feed.title: Fisho's Tackle World - Hervey Bay Weekly Fishing Report

entry.title: Fisho's Weekly Fishing Report – 23rd October, 2026
entry.content:
Caleb Pora was very happy with this fine 49cm jack. No doubt just one of many to come this spring.

Serious Rain – Seriously Unexpected

Wow! What was supposed to be a few showers and maybe a storm has developed into a major wet weather event for our region and many of our Queensland neighbours. So much for the super-dry El Nino eh! It is raining whilst writing this report and there is plenty more on the way apparently.

The weather is rather unappealing for boaties and landlubbers alike at present. Today's 15-20 knot north-easter is supposedly going to ease a tad tomorrow, but not by much. Expect at least 15 knots at times Saturday and more like 15-20 knots Sunday after the breeze tends more northerly. Showers, rain and the chance of storms all adding to a very gloomy weekend outlook.

The working week won't kick off much better either. Storms could roll in from out west, whilst showers blown onshore remain likely. The wind will still be quite stiff initially, from the north to north-west through Monday, before finally easing below 15 knots Tuesday. Who knows what the future thereafter might bring. It is indeed a stretch to forecast even a day or two ahead nowadays. So, batten down the hatches and settle in for a rather damp few days. As welcome as this rain is, too much right now would be very frustrating.

It is a crying shame that this weather event had to come at such a prime fishing time on our calendar. Tides are building whilst the moon is waxing as we approach Monday's full moon. There will be plenty of tidal flow and pretty high tides just due to the pull of the moon, so, even minor flooding will be exaggerated. Take care on our streams and be wary of approaching storms. Otherwise, catch up on your boat and tackle maintenance or drop in to Fisho's for some retail therapy if the weather and boredom get the better of you.

Hervey Bay local, Bob, enjoys his regular trips aboard Double Island Point Fishing Charters.

Les from Hervey Bay enjoying the snapper fishing offshore with Double Island Point Fishing Charters.

Post-Rain Action for Pier Fishos

As regular readers will all know, the pelagic scene at Urangan Pier has been pretty exciting lately. Broad-barred and school mackerel have been abundant and quite sizeable. GTs, queenfish and golden trevally have also turned up, along with stray barracuda, to feast on the abundance of herring (if not some of the lesser predators themselves).

Pelagic action may continue on and off after this round of building tides peak, but nonetheless there will be alternative target species worth pursuing due to the rains. The couple of jewfish that have been lurking beneath the pier and eluding capture could be joined by others, creating options for nocturnal fishos on both lures or live baits. Appropriately-weighted squid and prawn imitation softies will be most popular, as always, yet soft vibes could also be put to work on the jewies if you wish to experiment.

Flathead could gather in better numbers, if not drawn elsewhere by feeding opportunities created by local run-off. Joining them in either the first channel or out deeper could be a few stray grunter. There has been a few elsewhere within casting distance of landlubbers recently, and they will be on the chew around the full moon, so be prepared. Your next bait-tempted grunter might snavel a live herring, a simple squid or prawn bait, or a yabby meant for a whiting.

Oh, by the way, we have finally re-stocked with good numbers of beach worms just yesterday. Apologies to those of you that have come in looking for worms to chase whiting. This has been a challenging spring for local wormers and keeping product on our freezer shelves hasn't been easy. Doubly frustrating at the time of year when worms are so highly sought after.

Fisho's staffer, Jackson, doing what he does best - catching big flatties.

Jack Mostert calming down one of the big flathead he caught in the Mary prior to its release.

Fishing Local Run-off in the Rain

At the risk of jumping the gun, should this weather event bring sufficient falls to trigger any form of local run-off, then be prepared to pounce on the opportunities such an incident can bring. It could be as simple as sussing out the storm water outlets that pour out along our town beaches, fishing adjacent to creek mouths, or taking advantage of inflows in local pondages.

Our run of town beach whiting this season has been merely okay so far, with no truly impressive runs of fish to date. That situation could be morphing into a significant bite whilst you read this, as whiting gathered to spawn hit the feed button and go on the rampage.

Northerly winds pounding our north-facing beaches will stir those waters whilst the bigger tides create the current and scope the whiting so desire to feed. Add some run-off from pipes spewing all sorts of morsels across the beachscape and a feeding spree could be triggered. Conjecture? At this stage, yes, but go for a look and see what you find.

Should those pipes really get pumping, then you can add the chance of flathead, grunter and even queenfish to the list of potential predators lining up (albeit briefly) for a feed. Small sharks are just as likely too, so be a little wary of them if wading nearby. Even if the big rains don't materialise, those same areas adjacent to the outlets along our beaches are worth a visit. Maybe soak a couple of yabbies or a worm, or hop a small softie past a few times.

Hit the local pondages for something more serious if you are keen. Run-off pouring into these mini lakes can see predators lining up for an easy meal. We are talking barramundi and mangrove jacks now. Both species demanding tackle somewhat more substantial than whiting gear, yet not as heavy as you might think. With exceptions, there are lakes housing both species that offer little in the way of structure for them to trash you on, so it can be more a matter of appropriate leader for scuff-resistance, and a cool head and patience when connected to a trophy.

Certain lakes are totally fresh and host barra and mullet. One or two benefited from the midnight stocking group and carry a few bass. Others are fed by the tides, even if only on major moon phases, and host jacks as well as the barra and mullet. Cod, flathead and bream are also present adding to the variety you might encounter on various lures or baits. Tilapia have infected pretty much every local pond, and will spread their scourge should enough rain fall. Do not aid their cause by using them as live bait. It is totally illegal for a start, as is using cast nets in freshwater.

Fisho's staff member, Chewy, putting in some dedicated time chasing mangrove jacks in the Burrum.

One that didn't get away. This jack was unlucky not to bust Chris Ford off when it raced to a nearby snag after hook-up.

Reefies and Bay Pelagics Enjoy a Reprieve

As you can imagine, there has been very little boating and fishing effort in recent days other than in our estuaries. When you get the chance to head back out, there will be fresh fish that have moved about during the inclement weather. Such a weather pattern as this is bound to trigger a feeding response from many species, and very likely see a surge of fish onto our shallowest reefs.

Expect to catch coral trout in waters stirred-up by the onshore winds, and maybe good numbers of grassy sweetlip and grunter too. Once the northerlies abate, the likes of Gatakers Bay and Pt Vernon will be very popular, as will the bay islands. Trollers can get their game on, as can those who would rather catch their fish from a drifting or stationary boat.

Sharks are very likely to crash the party on our deeper inshore reefs, and maybe on some of our shallower ones too. Mackerel were abundant recently, and shouldn't be too hard to find. There were both broadies and schoolies off Pt Vernon recently, as well as over various reef systems from 'the banks' to the upper straits. Go for a troll or a spin post-wet and you will find them. Just concentrate on areas where baitfish numbers are strong.

Most recent reports from whale watch operators winding up their season suggest there is no snot weed issue to worry about in Platypus Bay, which is great news. You can head up the island looking for marlin as soon as this weather breaks. Going on results over the last new moon, you stand a very good chance of finding baby blacks somewhere in the northern sector of Platypus Bay, if not beyond Rooneys.

Mac tuna schools are being sighted more often out in the central bay and up the island. They are feeding on small baitfish at present, but not the tiniest tiddlers they will focus on soon. Baitfish in the 2-3-inch range are their main fodder for now, so tempting them with similar-sized metal slugs shouldn't be too hard. A handy side hustle between key marlin bite periods for those of you with kids keen on a little high-speed action.

Reports of three New Zealand fur seals in Hervey Bay were bouncing around the air waves last week, when whale watch operators spotted different animals in their travels. One particularly cheeky little fella seems to be lingering. He has been hitching a ride on more than one vessel, and is seemingly quite nonchalant about climbing aboard for a snooze. Avoiding our over-abundance of big sharks is probably a major part of his modus operandi, taking nothing from the cuteness overload.

It is great to observe the regenerative growth of our local sea grass beds after their depletion due to sediment and extended periods of turbidity from past wet seasons. Dugongs are relishing the renewed abundance, and are possibly the cause of mini-flotillas of busted sea grass infesting Urangan Harbour and nearby waters. It seems they chomp away at the stems, and the fronds float away (apparently). Hopefully our sea grasses can withstand the future flooding events when they occur, as the healthier these beds are, the healthier our waterways are in general.

Julie Brown enjoying the company of a furry hitchhiker along with her son Joey.

This NZ fur seal that hitched a ride with Joey Brown a few weeks ago has climbed onto Blue Dolphin two days in a row since.

How happy do you reckon Max Bradley was catching his maiden marlin whilst on holidays at Airlie Beach!

You can head offshore and catch kingies like this one. Or, you could just duck over to Kingfisher Bay Resort's jetty.

8 Days to Go to Catch Saltwater Barramundi

With the annual barramundi closed season looming, this weather is very likely to trigger a mad rush from local fishos keen to get amongst the barra while they still can. If it actually rains enough to trigger flooding, then that will be a gamechanger. But to date, there have been good numbers of barra scattered right through the mid-upper reaches of our rivers, as well as within many a creek system down the straits. Joining them has been small schools of quite large threadfin salmon as well, and both species will be supercharged by this weather.

Mangrove jacks fired up with warmer conditions a couple of weeks ago, yet remain just as likely to bite in cooler times such as now due purely to the nasty inclemency and the movement of baitfish and prawns such weather triggers. Take advantage of opportunities to fish the Burrum system for all three of the abovementioned species, as well as flathead, whiting, grunter and maybe a stray jewfish. Pelagics could even be an ongoing distraction well downstream if serious rains don't eventuate.

If you haven't caught a fingermark in our waters, then now and in coming weeks offers you a great chance. Debate over favoured tides will go on as differing folks discover the wonders of these fantastic lutjanids, but one constant will trigger opportunities. They will get the heck out of dodge should flooding even threaten, so you can tackle them before they do or intercept them whilst they do. You might fluke one whilst fishing for other species, but dedicated efforts will always be better rewarded. They aren't as rare as you might think in these parts, yet they are cunning and feed with specific focus.

Crabbers will be eyeing this weather; keen on a renewed abundance of mud crabs. We have just gone through the toughest mud crabbing period of the year, which is likely about to change due to this rain event. Muddies that crawled their way back into the hard-to-reach backwaters when salinity levels peaked will be flushed out if enough rain hits the ground. They will join the sandies in the straits at some time, which have been keeping crab fans fed in recent weeks.

Get out and into the salty barra fishos. You only have a week to catch fish like this one of Jack's.

Mark Williams was chuffed with this 80cm Mondy barra he caught on a Live Mullet lure.

Sean has been into a few salty barra. Something he and the rest of us won't be able to do come 1st November.

Tarj Wilson used a vibe to secure his PB threadfin salmon, proving these lures work just as well in the dark as they do the daylight.

Southern Straits & Offshore Wide Bay Fishing Well

Catching up for a chin wag with Greg Pearce from Double Island Point Fishing Charter fame this week was enlightening, as usual. Greg has been spending more time onshore than he would like this year, due simply to spells of weather too windy to let him head offshore. Weather permitting, the fishing offshore has been great, and Greg has been on the right spots to capitalise way more often than not.

The usual variety of quality reef fish have kept his clients keen, from fairly close inshore to way out wide where only deep dropping tackle can manage those depths. The current has been easily managed to date, though Greg mentioned it is building quickly beyond 15 miles offshore. Seemingly a month early, warm summer-like water is already pouring south out there, and is almost as warm, at a notable 24-25°C.

Water quality is excellent and the fish are abundant out off the Wide Bay bar, where sharks are only worst on larger reef systems and larger aggregations of fish. Being so familiar with the scene down there, Greg has been able to spot-hop to avoid depredation when necessary and continues to impress his clients with quality fish for them to catch and take home.

No mackerel down south to speak of as yet, with the best reports of spaniards still coming from up along Fraser's eastern side. The FADs off the southern end of Fraser are yet to produce any mahi mahi. Possibly due to the relative newness of these FADs and their lack of substantial marine growth to date. Mahi mahi are swimming in our offshore waters, as are yellowfin tuna, blue, black and striped marlin along the continental shelf. Exciting times ahead for heavy tackle game fishos when they can get back out wide.

Just one of many happy snaps from recent Double Island Point Fishing Charter trips.

Big sweeties and big pearlies often feature in catches from Double Island Point Fishing Charters.

Insights into the estuary scene at the southern extremities of the Great Sandy Straits suggest the sea grass beds are recovering just as well down there as they are up here. Barramundi numbers seem to be improving, which is excellent, as they join the usual long list of estuary predators and forage-feeders you can inspect from the straits. The jacks have come on the chew with recent warming, and are already showing signs of a great season.

Sand whiting in spawn-mode have been gathering in impressive numbers at Inskip Point as well as around the southern-most fringes of Fraser Island. They have not been easy to catch in daylight, as such spawn-focussed fish can be, but they are an impressive average size, well worthy of some effort on tides such as these right now. There has been plenty of sand crabs down south, as is the case throughout the rest of the straits up our way. Won't be long and the muddies will join them, or replace them, depending upon the volume of freshwater this weather event sends their way.

Quality tailor to 60cm or so and a few big dart have been caught south of the Maheno on Fraser Island's surf-side since the recent blow. A 'double beach' has formed, and wash-outs are common, so take care when driving. Inland tracks are all firm due to the rains, yet those from Kingfisher are rutted and mushy, with random holes full of water. Other tracks elsewhere are smooth with exposed roots.

What you have just read has been based on the potential of further significant rainfall. Totals exceeding 150mm have been recorded out Howard way, yet Lenthalls hasn't been over-topped. Minor rises have been declared in the Cherwell and sectors of the upper Mary River catchment, falling short of any 'flooding' status at this time.

Seems our parched landscape has soaked up much of the rain so far, which is fantastic. Some fresh will be evident in our rivers and streams, but nothing major at the time of writing. This week's totals nearing 100mm here in town have created brief run-offs and left our ground soaked. We are primed for some serious run-off if further heavy rains eventuate – let's see what unfolds.

Reds of this calibre are no. 1 on charter client wish lists. Getting on a Double Island Point Fishing Charter betters their chances.

Ado Kelly thoroughly enjoys his whiting fishing these days, and why wouldn't he when he comes home with a quality feed like this.

A traffic-free beach scene looking south from near Happy Valley this week. The season's biggest and best tailor are on offer right now.

Good luck out there y'all …… Jase

entry.title: Fisho's Weekly Fishing Report – 16th October, 2026
entry.content:
Dane was absolutely stoked with this beautiful permit he caught on fly whilst fishing at Weipa recently.

Onshore Breeze Bringing Showers

The weather has changed dramatically in recent days; from the previously steamy heat spawned by northerly winds to much cooler and breezier conditions with an increasing threat of showers. As pleasant and comfortable as our climate feels right now, it is hard to visualise any joy for boaties beyond sheltered waters for a few days to come.

Today's 15 knot easterly is set to strengthen slightly during Saturday and restrict boaties all weekend. Winds are likely to kick-off each day at 15 knots then build to 20 if not 25 knots. Saturday looks the worst, with a subtle improvement possible Sunday. The chance of showers is increasing day by day too. Not enough to soak our parched landscape, but welcome all the same if we can get a few mm per day.

Gradually improving weather into the next working week will open up opportunities for frustrated boaties. The high-pressure system that has stalled in the Tasman Sea will hopefully weaken enough to see winds lighten. Offshore will still be limited to larger vessels, but the eastern and southern bay should be okay.

The moon is waxing again after the passing of the new moon phase last Sunday. Monday will see in the half-moon of the latest first quarter phase, which means neap tides and minimal current flow once again. Happy days for those folks keen to tangle with our estuarine predators, but maybe not so brilliant for those limited to sheltered shallow reef fishing options or those keen to get amongst the beach whiting.

Ben Wall got stuck into the impoundment barra with the aid of Livescope.

Ben with another whopper. The Lake Monduran Family Fishing Classic is on this weekend, so expect chaos at the ramps and boats galore.

Variety of Pelagics Turning it on for Pier Fishos

An abundance of baitfish, that includes a welcome percentage of "surface herring", has been drawing the attention of many passing pelagic species to the waters beneath Urangan Pier. Surface herring are a particularly long and lean version of the genus in case you are wondering, much slenderer than greenbacks and most certainly more appealing to fish and fishos than "portholes". The surface herring are joined by hardy heads, and both are primo live baits for the big broad-barred mackerel haunting pier waters right now.

Broadies to beyond 9 kilos have been caught this week, with the average size keeping pier regulars coming back day after day. Joining their bigger cousins has been a consistent run of school mackerel. These are all legal fish too, with some sizeable specimens in the mix. Needless to say, Flasha spoon sales are spiking at Fishos once again, as keen mackerel fans get cranking.

Adding excitement and variety to the great run of mackerel has been a wave or two of large queenfish to 110cm and even a couple of golden trevally. Big ugly barracuda have been snatching mackerel mid-battle too, creating some memorable and equally frustrating moments for the anglers witnessing their attacks. Add the presence of a few large early-season GTs and you wouldn't want to be a mackerel or a baitfish anywhere near the Urangan Pier at present.

Somewhat less adrenalin-inducing, yet equally as appealing to other fishos, is the presence of quality flathead beneath the pier. A couple might be found along the slope into deeper water out near the end, with your chances about as good in the first channel. Make the effort to catch pike and deploy them alive to go one better on your competition attempting to tempt the same flatties with herring.

Dylan tricked this nice freshy into eating his softy during his latest pond mission.

Little miss Kreis with a fine bass she caught while fishing the fresh with her dad, Dylan.

Tarj scored his new PB flathead a mere cast away from the Burrum Heads boat ramp.

Tarj again with a beaut little barra from a local freshwater pondage.

Town Beach Whiting Fishery Not Living Up to Expectations

Every week can bring new hope and new expectations, but it is fair to say that our local town beach whiting fishery hasn't been as productive as it might be this season. Yes, there have been whiting caught, and reasonably regularly, but not in the numbers we (always) hope for this time of year.

Evening sessions saw the best catches over the past month, when tides were big enough. Last weekend's northerly wind was expected to spur a significant bite from fish gathering to feed in the more turbulent waters, but alas, numbers were less than expected. No shoulder-to-shoulder, everyone hauling them in scenes at the beach end of the Urangan Pier this year so far.

It seems it takes a little more than just the restrictions to gill-netting to bring back our whiting. Mother nature needs to play along as well. Local boaties that know what they are doing have been having no trouble scoring a bag limit of summeries on preferred tides elsewhere in the straits and along the western fringes of Fraser. Yet, here in town, the whiting numbers just aren't impressing.

Is our beachscape losing appeal to migrating whiting schools? Have we depleted our local population of yabbies too much? Is there too much bright light adversely affecting the passage of whiting? Maybe none of the above, maybe some, maybe other totally unrelated factors at play. Whatever the case, if you want a feed of whiting, then target them on prime tides and be prepared to keep mobile to find the best class of fish.

These neap tides do not qualify as prime when it comes to whiting. Next weekend will be much better. Having said this, you still remain a chance, and catching whiting big or small is always fun for the littler kids. Here is hoping this spell of onshore winds triggers a renewed migration along our town beaches and the next full moon fires big time, as the town beach whiting fishery can wind down somewhat thereafter.

Beau Muscat caught a couple of thumping big golden trevally during a recent bay mission.

Queenfish such as this one of Sean's are a great target species in the lower bay and the straits.

Shallow Reef Coral Trout and Mackerel Galore

Frustrated boaties that cannot head for more open waters will consider joining the usual fleet of tinnies off Gatakers Bay and Point Vernon this week. If they do, they will soon realise that the headland offers little protection from an easterly breeze. Regardless, we have transitioned into that time of year when the shallow water coral trout fishery ramps it up, so there will be crews trolling, crews flicking lures, and others soaking baits – all hoping for their share of an increasingly heavily-pressured resource.

Neap tides almost demand dawn starts and maybe even late finishes if you wish to get the best from the local trout. The lack of tidal flow will mean they will be a little lethargic and inclined to feed with less gusto, yet the wind itself can be a positive for those reef waters. Gathered baitfish can be a bite trigger, and wave action can create movement in the absence of tidal flow.

If trolling isn't appealing, then consider the simple art of flicking soft plastics for your next coral trout. You won't need especially heavy tackle for the class of fish that resides on these reefs these days, but you will still need sufficient stopping power (and quick reflexes). The ridiculous abundance of excellent soft plastic prawn imitations on offer these days is mind boggling. All potential coral trout lollies when attached to an appropriate jig head and twitched the right way.

Bait fishos might catch their next trout on a live bait, a whole pilchard, a hardy head, a herring or a whole banana prawn. Those same fishos might find a patch of grassy sweetlip worth processing too if they can avoid the tiddlers. Tusk fish, blackall, cod, perch and sharks are all possible too, whilst grunter could make an appearance. Like all shallow reef inhabitants, the local grunter will bite better with more run in the tide, but you never know your luck after dark during the neaps.

Mackerel have been quite abundant in the same area lately. Trollers are catching quality schoolies and broadies, and are even connecting to the odd stray spaniard. Bait fishos attempting to catch grunter from shore in the area pre-new moon were pestered by mackerel to such extent that it was either gear-up for them or move on – they were that hard to avoid. If you are a mackerel fan, then maybe a session at Gatakers out of the wind is an option this weekend.

Obviously, it is not just the Pt Vernon reefs that produce trout etc at this time of year. The onset of northerlies has ruffled the waters fringing the bay islands recently and turned the water quality more favourable for reef fish to return. Troll, flick or bait fish the fringing reefs surrounding Big Woody and the Picnics and you could expect better results than those fishing Pt Vernon – if you can handle the wind that is.

Brian picked up this ripper little black marlin near Rooneys after a fun trip offshore with Christian.

Just one of the marlin caught by Balin Whitford over the new moon prime bite period.

Baby Blacks Welcomed Back to Platypus Bay Waters

Probably the most exciting news this week would be the capture of multiple juvenile black marlin near Rooneys Point and Station Hill. It seems that a decent number of fish have turned up and the recent new moon really turned them on. This scene was kind-of expected, but challenging to predict, given the vagaries of weather, currents and fish migrations in past years. El Nino theories and history now come into play.

Congratulations to the crews that put in the effort last week. Just reward for being willing to head up there looking for the marlin without waiting for others to do the scouting. Successful crews raised several marlin; hooking some, losing some and landing some. One crew scored three fish for a session, whilst on another day, another crew scored five. Excellent results compared to last year, that's for sure.

So, perhaps your chance to troll those waters in peace is long gone, but you can head up towards Rooneys with great confidence of raising billfish whenever this weather settles enough. The current wind scenario is unlikely to phase those on larger vessels given the inherent protection that Fraser Island offers, and even vessels under 5m can take on the challenge if the skipper and crew are willing to cop a little pounding on the way to the island.

Drop in and see the lads at Fishos if you need advice on catching your first Hervey Bay marlin. We are stocked-up with all the best skirts, along with custom rigs to suit. Bait-rigging arsenal is readily available as are the "fresh frozen" garfish you will need to be rigging if you go the bait option. Be prepared to dish out for a decent teaser set-up if you are in anyway serious, as drawing the marlin to your spread of lures is a must to get a bite.

Ensure you have a suitable spinning outfit at the ready too; armed with a large jerkbait-style plastic, a rigged garfish, or a hook ready to pin one of the live yakkas swimming in your bait tank. Being so prepared gives you the option to pitch a bait or lure at a lit-up billy that won't commit to the skirts in your spread. Be ready to drag that teaser away from the cheeky little buggers too, as these little juvies can get excited and try to eat anything that looks like tucker.

Whale watching crews have once again mentioned free-jumping billfish in their travels this week. The fact that local whale boats will end their season in a week or so due to the downturn in humpback numbers is likely great news for boaties keen to wander the bay with less hazards. We all love our whales, of that there is no doubt, but their numbers are making many skippers extra-nervous nowadays.

The snot weed issue reported on recently is luckily not affecting the marlin grounds in northern Platypus Bay at present. There could be lingering issues further south or in the central bay, so move elsewhere if you run into any. The weed was bad enough to clog water intakes on whale boats and on outboard engines only a week ago, so good riddance to it.

There are big golden trevally harassing bait schools off Rooneys Point and plenty of their smaller second cousins lurking around bait-rich reefs further south in Platypus Bay. Mac tuna schools are quite obvious when busting up on the tiny baitfish they prefer. That tiny bait biomass will increase over the coming month or so and draw spotties and more tuna our way. Until then, you might as well chase mackerel that are feasting on larger baits such as herring and yakkas whilst they remain so abundant.

A sample of a perfect starter kit for those of you keen to gear-up for your first Hervey Bay light tackle marlin.

You want gear for marlin - we have all you need, right here at Fisho's.

Pursuing Pelagics Offshore

This weather will limit all but the biggest game boats from heading for offshore waters, but it cannot hurt to look back on last week's efforts. The Coral Reef Fin Fish Closure impacted northern bay waters and the grounds north-east of Fraser, so reef fishing took a back seat to trolling and a little selective deep dropping for crews that made the effort.

Heavy tackle black marlin were raised and lost by one crew, whilst another crew managed the capture of at least one blue marlin. Yellowfin tuna bycatch was encountered whilst trolling in 200m of water, with no birds in sight. The best of the 'fin went a credible 40 kilos or so, whilst it seems all the tuna bettered 30 kilos at least.

Driven by limited success trolling the shelf, one skipper steered back to the shoal country where poppers were put to work on the spanish mackerel and giant trevally. This was after the same crew decided a feed of deep water reefies was a good idea and the deep dropping tackle was brought out. The skipper knew grounds that only hold snapper and pearl perch, so knew he wouldn't be tampering with coral reef species, and proceeded to slip some very nice pearlies into the esky. Yellowtail kingfish around the 15-kilo mark also took their baits, putting a nice bend in the bent-butts without challenging that sort of serious tackle.

From what we hear, the 4-mile bar crossing is somewhat closed out at present and proving a bit risky. A shift to a gutter formed at what you might call the 6-mile is vastly safer and a better crossing, as of last weekend. There will be a lot more traffic up that way when the weather improves, so we will endeavour to bring you the latest on the bar and the fishing offshore when to hand.

George and Brian hitched a ride with Christian and got amongst the yellowfin tuna along the continental shelf whilst trolling for marlin.

George and the spoils of a deep dropping session during the CRFF closure on grounds skipper Christian was confident held no coral reef fin fish.

A River System or the Straits – Options Out of the Wind

Boaties must concede to the weather and opt for safety, so some may take on the straits this week, whilst others stick with the rivers. Waters temperatures spiked last week while the heat prevailed. Even though it is cooler again, any temperature decline will only be subtle, so all the springtime predators will still be catchable.

Kingfisher Bay Resort's jetty is playing host to numbers of school mackerel at present. Chances are, broadies might even pay a visit too, given how many are only mere miles away near Urangan. Sight-fishing for flathead from the same jetty is a favoured pastime of regulars and first-time visitors, who can try and catch them on soft vibes, but will typically do best with live baits.

Neap tides aside, the Great Sandy Straits' population of quality grunter is worth pursuing. Find them in the creeks, in the channels and along the ledges fringing Fraser's western shores. Chase flathead as well if you wish, by focussing around creek mouths and adjacent mangrove verges hopping your favourite new flathead lollies.

Mangrove jacks in Fraser's western creeks were a better proposition last week with the peaking heat, but they are pretty much a day-to-day option from now until the wet season rains come regardless. Barra and threadies will be hotly pursued this week no doubt, and both species can be found in numerous creek systems as well as select hotspots beyond the streams.

There is only two weeks to go before you can no longer fish for saltwater barramundi for 3 months, so make the most of this week if you can. The Mary's barra are being pursued regularly, as are the Burrum's, yet both systems remain sound options this week. Focus on the threadies in those same rivers prior to the tide slackening for the last of the ebb and your downtime will be limited.

Tie on smaller lures and go see if the Burrum's mangrove jacks are still keen to party after the peak bite during the hot new moon period. Slower-moving water will certainly make it easier to present your lures to likely jack lairs; they just might take a few more casts to respond. Persist in cooler conditions like this by peppering grounds you are confident jacks are holding in and the bites will come, eventually. If not, then come back at night with topwater lures.

River grunter and whiting bit better last week than they will this week, due to the neaps. They are there though, so don't write them off, particularly after dark. Woodgate Beach fished very well for whiting last week by the way. Shore-based fishos scored excellent whiting in numbers and picked up some fine flathead too. The Burrum's flathead are copping a touch-up yet there are still ample fish to target if that option appeals.

Mud crabbing remains quite challenging, as it should at this driest time of year. Future storms will see the crabs hunted from their present backwater lairs when sufficient run-off drives them out. But for now, you will have to get pretty muddy to get your pots to the better crabs. Sandies are an easier option down the straits, and will be a possibility in open waters of the bay soon too, once the whales depart the bay.

Avalon Russell was very happy to catch this fine grunter while fishing with her dad, Rick.

Matt Cawley and his latest threadfin salmon capture. These will be an easy target species this weekend.

Time to Catch Fraser's Biggest Greenback Tailor

Sadly, we haven't been able to gain much information on the success or otherwise of the headland fishery on Fraser Island since the annual fishing closure concluded 1st October. If the observations of the crew from Maryborough's Colts Mens Hockey Club that were there during the last week of the closure is anything to go by, then it must have been fantastic.

That crew climbed the headlands and spent some fascinating time from an elevated position above Middle Rocks as well, to watch massive schools of tailor milling about below. Skirting the fringes of the tailor schools and actively predating on them were numbers of big giant trevally and spanish mackerel. Sharks were abundant too unfortunately, but certainly added another level of excitement to the chaotic scenes unfolding before them.

Their whole crew enjoyed excellent tailor fishing during their stay. The building tides fished well into the evening. Stickbaits produced some of the better-quality tailor, even though the lads didn't catch any whoppers over 60cm. Baits produced plenty of tailor too, with large garfish out-classing the standard pillies for quality.

Ignoring the tales of woe from so many other crews on the island, this intrepid well-experienced crew found tailor everywhere they looked, and even scored a nice feed of whiting from a gutter near Waddy Point. They caught mullet from the same gutter on both worms and pippies, which was as much a surprise as a bonus.

After eating all their fish fresh on the island, one member of the crew stopped at a gutter at Yidney Rocks on the way home and landed an impressive 20 tailor in an hour on Shimano Spin Beam metal slugs he found in a dump bin here at Fisho's. Amazing fishing and a great week for all involved. Well done lads, and thanks Andrew for the report.

Since the closure, folks fishing gutters in the central sector found a good class of greenback tailor when conditions were favourable, along with a few feisty trevally. This onshore breeze has upset the apple cart over there for now, but with any luck, it will flatten the beach out a bit. There are some pretty nasty wash-outs on a rather lumpy beach right now, so take extra care while travelling.

There will be folks keen to hit Fraser's tailor at the tail end of the season when the biggest fish are there for the taking. Better weather will help those folks, as will the option to target them with stickbaits cast across gutters or from the headlands. Drone fishos and slide-baiters will be keen to get their baits back out in better conditions too, wondering whether the next monster to tear line from their spool will be a big spaniard, a GT or yet another shark. Exciting times ahead for some lucky Fraser Island fishos no doubt.

Andrew Davies with 20 tailor caught on his way home from an excellent week on Fraser.

Andrew took out the prize for the biggest tailor caught on a penis lure during the latest Colts Mens Hockey Club Fraser trip.

Quality greenbacks are being caught on Fraser's surf-side. The best fish in this photo went a whopping 66cm.

Good luck out there y'all …… Jase

Get ready to party game fishos. The HBGFC's biggest event of the year isn't far away.

entry.title: Fisho's Weekly Fishing Report – 9th October, 2026
entry.content:
Joe with a mammoth bluey that made it past the sharks.

Classic Mid-Spring Weather this Week

Having missed last week's report due to a pesky wog, there are a few new topics to write about this week. Weather-wise it has been a fairly typical kick off to October and the unofficial start to our storm season. Northerly winds are set to dominate this weekend and into early next week, so it will be warm, yet rather pleasant.

This morning's light easterly will tend north to north-easterly and strengthen to 15 knots as the afternoon unfolds, setting the stage for the weekend. Northerly winds around 10-15 knots can be expected both Saturday and Sunday. Most likely gentler in the mornings and building to a typical sea breeze in the afternoons.

Days will be warmer, with the evening temperatures noticeably higher. Expect more of the same light-moderate northerly breeze into the early working week, prior to a showery change mid-week. Very much typical mid-spring weather for these parts, and rather welcome, as we shake off the cooler months and enjoy the ultimate climate before the heat takes hold.

The weather offshore off Sandy Cape looks fantastic for game fishos heading wide for marlin. Bash your way through the slop on the bay and you will find better weather outside Sunday through Tuesday. The northerly will increase drift rates for reef fishos, but trollers will revel in the great conditions over tides and a moon most suitable for catching our mighty billfish.

There is substantial current flow right now as our tides build towards this Sunday's new moon. The tides aren't massive, but still offer enough variation to trigger substantial movement from many of our piscatorial friends, meaning a potentially great bite from a host of species from whiting, flathead and grunter to billfish, mackerel, snapper and shallow water coral trout.

Deej hit a freshwater pondage and got into some feisty barra on jighead flies using Livescope.

John Browne with most of a nice trout he managed to wrestle away from a little noah at the Gutters.

Reed Winch caught this grunter on the well-proven GULP Shrimp softy.

Reed again with another grunter. This time on the Rapala Crush City Imposter. Well done young man.

Mackerel Have Urangan Pier Fishos Spinning Flat-out

Following a fairly exciting time on Urangan Pier for holidaying school kids, the local pier regulars have been having a ball out there chasing pelagics ever since. There is plenty of herring sheltering beneath the pier, and this shimmering biomass has been the drawcard for numbers of mackerel.

The herring may be abundant, but they have been challenging to catch at times apparently. Luckily for most regulars, they are always armed with an assortment of metal spoons and slugs, so they happily spin for the mackerel while they are so prolific. Flasha spoons in the 35 and 50 gram sizes remain the weapons of choice for pier fishos (and local boaties) when it comes to tempting the toothy critters.

Whilst school mackerel have been quite consistent in recent weeks, it is the arrival of big numbers of broad-barred mackerel that really has the pier fishos excited. Broadies in the 3-9 kilo range have been caught daily of late, whilst a couple of regulars have racked up substantial daily tallies. This run won't last forever, so get out there asap if you wish to join in the fun.

Distractions from the mackerel included occasional passing schools of mac tuna recently, along with the chance of flathead from the first channel. Shark fishing after dark is becoming more popular as our waters warm, meaning extra effort can be expected in coming weeks and months before the crowds descend for the summer pencil squid season.

Deej found the Livescope useful when targeting our local threadies.

Jeff with a recent estuary cod capture. These fish are hyperactive this time of year and reside on every other bit of reef we have.

Josh Downing hit the fresh and got amongst the Mary's sooty grunter.

Josh Cox getting up close and personal with his latest grunter capture.

Northerly Winds and New Moon Mean Whiting Time

No doubt there will be a few fishos taking advantage of the good tides, weather and time of year to pursue whiting from the beach end of the Urangan Pier this week. Nocturnal efforts have been very rewarding for nearby beach fishos on less appealing tides recently, so this northerly breeze and the bigger new moon tides should have an even better class of whiting on the chew.

Remembering that the northerly creates the turbulence and discolouration of the water that enables the whiting to mooch up into the shallows comfortably to feed should create just the recipe for a much-improved daytime whiting bite. Try the latter half of the rising tide and the first of the ebb for best results, anywhere from the Urangan Pier to the Torquay jetty. The groynes at Shelly Beach will be a popular platform for some, whilst others wander the nearby beachscape looking for a better class of fish.

Pump some yabbies to use alive if you have a yabby pump and can get to the yabby banks at low tide. Otherwise, drop in for the next best thing, in the form of cured worms at Fishos. Sourcing beach worms has been rather challenging this spring, as regular suppliers run dry. We have ample in stock once again right now though.

The Hervey Bay Amateur Fishing Club's 6th annual Junior Whiting Fishing Competition held a couple of Saturdays ago was a resounding success by the way. Organisers were overwhelmed with the turn-out of kids and their supporting family members, and actually had to contend with way more folks than they had anticipated. Some lovely whiting were caught by the kids and they pretty much all had a ball. The whiting fishing has improved further since then, so this weekend is another opportunity to get the kids amongst the whiting while this most convenient fishery lasts.

The Toogoom Family Fishing Competition was held two weekends ago too and was a tremendous success. Lots of fish were weighed in, both live and dead. All categories were filled and winners declared at the final ceremony that saw lots of happy winners walking away with arms full of prizes. This event was particularly family-focussed and ensured that the kids had a great time. Well done to the organisers and congratulations to all the winners.

Toogoom Fishing Club's Family Fishing Comp was a great success. Fun times for the kids during the school holidays.

The kids weighed in plenty of fine fish in the recent Toogoom Fishing Classic and were rewarded with some beaut prizes.

All the winners from the recent Toogoom Family Fishing Competition.

Coral Reef Fin Fish Closure in Force

Missing last week's report meant we couldn't forewarn you of the upcoming Coral Reef Fin Fish Closure that actually commenced yesterday. This is the first of two five-day closures that impact waters north of latitude 24°50' south. This closure runs through October 8th to 12th inclusive, with the upcoming November closure being from the 6th to the 10th inclusive.

During the closure, you are not permitted to catch any species listed in the Coral Reef Fin Fish Plan. This includes coral trout variants, many cod, emperors, job fishes, parrot, tusk fishes, sweetlips and perches. There is other 'rocky reef' or 'other tidal species' that you can target, but few would make the effort to fish reef waters during this period regardless. Given that the closure has been deemed necessary to protect our treasured reef species in their recognised prime spawning times, we trust that all of you will do the right thing and leave them in peace.

This closure only affects the most northerly waters of Hervey Bay, so you can still fish for the same species south of the abovementioned latitude. I have lamented this fact year in year out for some time now; pointing out that the very same species south of a given latitude deserve the same protection as their northern cousins. Yet alas, the status quo remains unchanged, and our local trout etc will have to go about their spawning activity under the usual immense pressure that is the South East Queensland fishery.

Having said this, the fact is that this time of year and these very tides are the kick-starter to our inshore shallow reef trolling season. The north wind might spook a few folks this weekend, but those with past runs on the board will be fully aware of the results they can expect from new moon trolling efforts over our shallow fringing reefs. Coral trout will always be the number one target of course, though a little bycatch in the form of cod, perch, mackerel and grunter can be anticipated.

Word from folks attempting to extract a feed of reef fish from our deeper inshore reef systems has been a little daunting of late. Many are saying that they simply cannot get a fish past the sharks, whilst occasionally someone mentions scoring a feed with little attention from the noahs. Needless to say, minimise your impact on our inshore reef fishery by steering away from sites relentlessly hounded by sharks, and bounce from spot to spot to extract a feed, as is the sad norm of the modern day.

Caleb headed offshore with the old man and got amongst some big fat pearlies.

Rob managed to haul this great-looking coral trout from its lair on a recent reef mission.

Chris with a ripper red caught on a recent trip off 1770 with Aedan.

Georgia joined Garry Harman on a recent trip to 1770 and caught this most impressive red emperor. Awesome fish, well done.

Time to Gear-Up for Marlin

If history is anything to go by, then the new moon in October offers a prime opportunity to go hunting marlin within Hervey Bay, and beyond. Recent efforts and sightings suggest there are at least a few fish cruising the waters of Platypus Bay, so take advantage of the moon and tides if you, your vessel and crew can handle a little northerly slop.

We have just restocked our game fishing arsenal at Fishos with all the right skirts, pre-made rigs, teasers and other paraphernalia you will need for successful days hunting billfish. Light tackle is the go for bay waters, so we have oodles of product adorning our walls to choose from that is quite obvious. We also happen to have a selection of heavy tackle lures and hardware stashed out the back that is just awaiting a wall revamp to display for all to see.

This season's heavy tackle season is underway. Blacks and stripes caught along the continental shelf east of Breaksea Spit and Fraser Island will be joined by big blues at some time, and local game fishing crews will all of a sudden be sharing our waters with gun game boats from afar. Exciting times ahead for offshore crews sporting both heavy and light tackle, where plenty of bycatch can be expected as well as the billies in coming weeks and months.

Worth noting perhaps; that there is a trawl closure in place that commenced 20th September and runs for 6 weeks. This is of most interest to offshore fishos keen to go reef fishing (when the Coral Reef Fin Fish Closure isn't in force). Sharks are bad enough offshore at the best of times, so you can imagine how many more there are out there right now without trawlers to follow around.

There is still an issue with 'snot weed' in Hervey Bay waters by the way. Worth avoiding if you are into any form of fishing, let alone trolling. It will be fairly obvious in the water should you wander into an affected area, so steer away to avoid the menace if you need to. Last reports suggest the central northern bay might still be affected, but the worst of the snotty stuff is in the southern and eastern bay north of 'the banks'. Be wary of this stuff clogging your engine's water intakes folks, it is that thick in places.

There are mac tuna up the island for anyone keen to put the kids onto them for a little high-speed fun. Larger longtails are few and far between, but there has been the odd fish caught deep in the water column on baits or lures meant for other species. Trevally schools up that will keep them entertained on jigs and softies otherwise, so long as you avoid the areas affected by snot weed.

School mackerel have been thrilling holidaymakers and others around local beacons lately. The same fish can be found by trolling the shipping channels, or by spinning for them over reef systems alive with baitfish. Broadies closer inshore and a stray spaniard or two have joined good numbers of school mackerel off Pt Vernon, so you won't have to burn much fuel to bring home some product for the smoker box.

A few giant trevally, queenfish and mackerel are taking advantage of clearer waters in our estuary systems and venturing well into our rivers in some cases. Whilst mostly smaller models of the GTs and queenies are expected, there are quite large GTs wandering the waters of the mighty Mary at present, whilst schools of similarly large brutes have been spotted not far from the mouth of the Burrum. These bruisers will eat anything that fits in their gob, so Burrum Head's run of school mackerel might be on the menu.

Jagger living up to his moniker whilst trolling with Luke off Gatakers Bay recently.

Luke has been trolling up plenty of big schoolies off Pt Vernon.

Jesse and one of the trout caught fishing our fringing shallow reefs with a 'Live Shrimp' softy.

Prawn imitation softies are the gun lures for shallow water coral trout. Just ask CJ.

Boat Ramp Upgrade and New Beacons in the Mary

Signs in place at River Heads boat ramp advertise that the end of the consultation period for proposed upgrade works to the River Heads boat ramp facilities is nigh. You only have until this Sunday 11th October to have your say. So, jump online and find the survey form etc and let the Qld government know your thoughts on this incredibly important piece of local infrastructure.

I won't try and influence any of you, but would encourage you to have your say. There are any number of concerns that regular boaties could readily raise. One rather obvious one might be to at least place the poles on the appropriate side of the pontoon for a start!

If you haven't made a dash up the Mary for a while, then you are bound to notice recent movements of navigational beacons, as well as a few brand-new ones. A couple of these have been placed in situ just recently it seems, so familiarise yourself with the new placements next time you head upstream (or seek out the latest Notices to Mariners that declare the changes).

Fishing-wise it has been all about chasing barramundi and threadfin salmon for a large cohort of the boats on the Mary. It's a race to the hotspots some days, where recent pressure becomes obvious for those that turn up after the weekend's efforts. All-in-all, there are a few of the usual spots hosting barra, while threadies remain fairly mobile and in vastly less numbers than they have been in numerous past years. What the threadies appear to lack in number, they make up for in size at least, so trophies are on offer for those that refine their search and can tempt them to bite.

Grunter are mooching well upstream as well, holding in the usual locations sporting gravelly bottom, shell grit and the like. These bigger tides will favour grunter hunters more than those chasing the bigger estuary predators, though everyone is in the race at low tide at least. As the tides fully drain you will notice a smattering of quality prawns, most likely as they are being chased by a sambo or barra. Not hard to guess what food source you should be mimicking.

Stay well downstream and you can catch an excellent feed of whiting. There are both sand and northern whiting in the river at present, whilst winteries can be found in decent numbers mere miles beyond the river mouth too. Talk of weed impacting whiting grounds out in the straits is par for the course for this time of year. It isn't everywhere, so move to avoid the weed if you must.

Some fun with flatties is an option in the lower reaches of the Mary and Susan and most certainly throughout the straits. Look for them near obvious ambush points during the ebb tide and then again up on the flats as the tide is flooding. If you are carrying anything resembling heavy topwater tackle, then maybe you could toss some poppers or stickbaits around the swirling current lines near the heads (or beyond). Those GTs mentioned earlier are a possibility over these darks.

There are a couple of serial pests wandering the waters of the Mary and the Great Sandy Straits. The biggest and baddest is the nasty old bull sharks of course; turning up all too regularly when quality threadfin salmon and other fish are hooked. Their junior offspring annoying bait fishos trying to fish livies for more desirable predators.

More annoying to bait fishos, but most certainly worth avoiding by all are the dreaded green toads. Those blighters are well upriver and quite prolific within many a creek system down the straits. Terrible critters that can not be deterred, only avoided, so do yourself and your tackle collection a favour and drive away from them if they find you.

You could try and catch some muddies this week, but you will be faced with one of the tougher times of year. Water clarity and salinity suggest those poking beyond comfortable waters into the hard-to access gullies will do best. Sand crabs are a better option if you head for the straits. Quality sandies are feeding crews down there that wouldn't dare run their pots in open bay waters due to the potential of entanglement with humpbacks.

Daiwa's new Bait Junkie 4'' Prawn softy getting the job done on the Mary's big threadies.

Threadfin salmon coloration varies from drab grey to bright gold, even in the same schools.

You can catch a lot of flathead in our estuaries at present. Deej has been into them, grunter and threadies lately.

You can also pick up a nice feed of grunter in our creeks and rivers right now. Great tides for this weekend.

Prime Time to go Chasing Mangrove Jacks

Northerly winds, a spike in evening temperatures and a new moon all combine to create an exciting recipe for primo mangrove jack fishing. We all know jacks love the warmth, but they also love the darks, where their big old eyes give them a substantial advantage over their prey whilst hunting at night.

Prone to wander liberally well away from their lairs during the dark nights of the new moon, big bruiser creek jacks can be targeted in all sorts of ways by those keen to brave the nocturnal estuary scene. Undoubtedly those with the easiest and perhaps best chance are those favouring baits such as fresh mullet fillets, whole poddies and live prawns, whilst the bigger new moon tides challenge lure fishos.

Notwithstanding, topwater options are boundless at this time. River and creek waters are quite clear, so various presentations, both subtle and noisy can work. Some may favour poppers, whilst others of us will stick with our trusty fizzers. If walking the dog is more your thing, then get that stickie dancing across rock bars or past back eddies and wait for the peace-shattering crunch that only a jack attack can emulate.

The sand flies and mozzies are just plain nasty in our creeks and rivers right now, and this element seemingly adds to potential success whilst chasing jacks. If storms start to brew, or even a thundery shower appears, then late afternoon sessions can be extra special this time of year. That's when those big old jack eyes go looking for their next victim without the glare of the sun they spend so much time hiding from.

The Burrum system is obviously a great option given its huge population of jacks. So too, the many creeks dotted along the western fringe of Fraser Island. Creeks quite close by that seem innocuous and unproductive at a glance in daylight can really turn it on after dark. Some of the very same creeks offer excellent jack fishing during the daylight hours too potentially, so long as your timing sees you plying your craft when the water isn't flooded well up into the mangroves.

Jacks demand a special level of skill to catch that can not be boosted as easily with technology the way barra fishing and thready fishing can. Our waters teem with some of the classiest and just plain old nastiest jacks in Qld. Even our piddling little creeks can host 50cm+ fish, whilst the Burrum and many a spot down the straits sport tackle-busting brutes beyond the legendary 60cm mark. This is the perfect weekend to test your skills against a most worthy adversary. You just need to learn where jack lives.

Good luck out there y'all …… Jase

Dax and the results of another spearing session.

entry.title: Fisho's Weekly Fishing Report – 25th September, 2026
entry.content:
Brax Empson scored his first-ever Mondy barra at a whopping 108cm. Excellent fish mate, well done.

Winds Easing for the Full Moon

The September school holidays kicked off nicely with some very pleasant weather and ample opportunity for boaties to head far and wide. That joy was short-lived however, as a rather gusty south-easter took hold mid-week and stifled boaties' plans for a few days.

Today's 20-knot south-easter is expected to ease a tad overnight and tend more east to south-easterly at around 15 knots for Saturday. Both days offering a slight chance of a shower if we get lucky. Sunday is looking absolutely brilliant. Barely 10 knots from either side of easterly will greet boaties on waters more likely to get lumpy from all the holiday traffic than the winds. Clear skies and a full moon too – just about perfect!

Monday offers decent conditions early, before the breeze picks up that afternoon. There is another brief spike of onshore south-easterly expected that night, that will keep everyone onshore awaiting the next lull. What happens thereafter is anyone's guess, as the weather gurus have changed their forecasts radically a couple of times in the last 24 hours.

Sunday's full moon means our tides are peaking once again. Nothing massive by local standards at 3.7m from 0.5m, but enough tidal movement to trigger a feeding response from many foraging and predatory species. Enough of a tidal drain to catch unfamiliar boaties unawares too, so take extra care if pumping yabbies, lingering in Fraser's western creeks or up on our vast sand/mud flats this weekend. These big tides can trap folks during holiday times.

Leo Arnold has gone next level, catching this 14kg+ red on his dad's stand-up Daiwa Seaborg 500MJ electric combo. Wow lad!

Robbie Muller was chuffed with this brace of quality reds.

Pier Pelagic Action Exciting for Holidaying Kids

Just as it so often does, the Urangan Pier fishery has turned it on for the September school holidays. Masses of baitfish are entrenched beneath the pier and drawing the attention of plenty of passing pelagics.

Longtail tuna made another appearance or two while the tides still suited them, then the broad-barred mackerel showed up for the neaps. School mackerel have been relatively constant, but their numbers still vary day to day. At least they are of improving size, so the kids have been having fun spinning for them with Flasha spoons and the like.

The odd flathead thrilled onlookers as it was spotted then hauled over the rails on live bait while the tides weren't too strong. Flatties are a chance on virtually any tide, but they do favour those first making tides after the half-moon. Night time has been shark time, or otherwise a time for those learning the intricacies of the pier nocturnal fishery.

Included in that nocturnal learning could be a session catching whiting from the beach end of the pier. Negating the need for the long walk to the deep end suits many a family fisho weighed down with all the paraphernalia necessary to take toddlers fishing these days.

The latter half of the rising tide and the first of the ebb are whiting prime times for pier or beach-goers. This weekend's full moon tides are optimal, so take the kids for a late afternoon orientation that extends into the evening (or line them up for a mid-morning session if that is more appealing). Evenings will be better due to our prevailing water clarity, but both tides can be productive.

Chris Ross took out the 1st and runner-up 'parrot' prizes at Woodgate with ripper venus tuskfish like this one.

Chris joined the chase for prizes in the red emperor category at the Woodgate Classic with this nice schoolie.

You can imagine Kevin's surprise (and subsequent exhaustion) after hooking this big GT near River Heads.

Mark Whitford sampled Mondy's barra fishing recently. It is hectic up there at present and going to be crazy busy this weekend.

HBAFC Junior Whiting Competition this Saturday

Go one better and take the kids along for the Hervey Bay Amateur Fishing Club's 6th Annual Junior Whiting Fishing Competition this Saturday at Lower Dayman Park in Urangan. Kicking off at 7.30am, this free event is a very popular one amongst local families and visitors alike, and is timed perfectly to take advantage of an expected full moon run of whiting along our town beaches.

You need to gear them up with their own rod and reel, some terminal tackle, bait and a bucket. All the other usual stuff required to keep them sun-smart and hydrated will ensure they are focussed on the fishing for the hours preceding the sausage sizzle and prize-giving ceremony around 11am. Enlist the help of the on-hand fishing club members should you or your kids need some guidance, and get the kids participating in the other activities should they not be engaged by a great whiting bite.

Obviously, you can come and see us at Fisho's for your bait and tackle requirements before the event. Our usual bait supplier is struggling to keep up with demand for beach worms at this time, so we have ordered some from another supplier to fill the current and untimely void in our shop freezer. Grab some before they run out, as chasing whiting will be a very popular activity this week.

Deej with the class of whiting it took to win the top prizes in the whiting category at Woodgate.

Estuary cod are prolific in our waters, from the creeks to the reefs. Get the kids onto them on jigged or trolled lures, live baits or whole squid.

Mac tuna are great fun for the kids and a Hervey Bay staple you can always find busting up somewhere in the bay.

Not a great photo, but a fantastic capture! Young Marlon caught his namesake on Saturday when others struggled.

Toogoom Family Fishing Classic this Weekend

It is almost a given that a number of the kids and their families that enjoy the Junior Whiting Comp will roll up to register for Toogoom Fishing Club's annual Family Fishing Classic that very same afternoon. A massive early bird prize is up for grabs for anyone registering before 3pm Saturday, so get in early and you could be a winner before you even catch a fish.

Fishing is open from 3pm today (Friday) and concludes this Sunday at 12 noon. There are oodles of prizes up for grabs, that include a motza of fishing tackle supplied by Fisho's Tackle World. Lots of activities will keep the kids entertained at the site when not fishing, that include mud crab races, a colouring-in competition, and plenty more the club has instore for them Saturday night.

Offering prizes for biggest fish, runner-up and secret weights means many folks can end up winning multiple prizes. Some of those are a fist full of cash too, so make sure you weigh-in your catch even if you don't think you have the species winner. The kids can target specific species that include whiting, bream, flathead, garfish and flounder. There are separate junior prizes for fish weighed-in live and for those weighed-in dead.

Adults can focus on catching whiting, bream, flathead, grunter, mangrove jack, grassy sweetlip and pelagics. Adults' fish can be weighed in either live or dead (with the exception of flathead that are live-weigh only). Unlike the kids' prize pool, live and dead weigh-ins are competing with each other for the same prizes. This could mean that a whiting of a given weight weighed live would beat a similar fish weighed-in dead as the dead fish would need to be gilled and gutted. Encouragement right there for competitors to bring their fish to the weighmaster live if they possibly can.

Weigh stations will alternate between the Toogoom Community Hall and the Toogoom Boat Ramp. See the leaflet at the end of this report for guidance and weigh-in times, or jump online and google the event for more details. This is bound to be a fun event for quite a crowd of families this weekend. We wish you all the best of luck and hope you and your kids score your share of the prizes.

Beelbi Creek at Toogoom is ultra-clear and supporting a significant biomass of herring right now by the way. Masses of tucker to draw the attention on passing pelagics such as queenfish, and to feed the semi-resident barra, jacks, cod and flathead. The whiting are biting in the creek too, even though most are falling short of 30cm to date. Every chance a better class of whiting will turn it on for the full moon and hopefully feature in the weigh-ins at the comp.

Dane from Fisho's teaching the littl'ns the finer arts of casting at the Woodgate Classic.

Kids enjoying the Tackle World DIY lure-painting kits at Woodgate.

Shimano's Fish Fighting Simulator was a big hit with the kids at the Woodgate Classic.

Party time at Woodgate Beach Hotel during the Classic. Over 1,000 competitors vied for $200,000+ in prizes and had a ball.

Woodgate Beach Fishing Classic a Roaring Success

Talk to anyone that attended the Woodgate Beach Fishing Classic last weekend and they will tell you they had a ball. How would they not, with such a well-run comp drawing such a massive crowd of like-minded people all hell-bent on showing their families a great time in an atmosphere alive with laughs and convivial banter.

There were some 1005 entrants this year, swelling the comp to absolute maximum capacity. There were around 250 kids in that number, and there is no doubt that they all relished the fun and games. There was the Shimano Fish Fighting Simulator displayed for all to see on the big screen, plus cart races, a casting accuracy competition, and oodles more activities to exhaust the kids on their Big Day Out on Saturday.

Big nights might've made for a few grizzles and delayed departures the next morning no doubt, yet the huge fleet of competitors scattered far and wide and brought back some very impressive fish. There were fish caught from over the bar off Breaksea, from the northern bay and all over Hervey Bay and within our estuaries closer to home. Way too many to list here, so suss out the Leader Board from the Classic's website hereabouts, or slip online and check out the long lists of names that weighed-in fish category by category.

This Woodgate Classic just gets bigger and better year by year, and is a must-attend for many returnees regardless of the weather. This year's event was an absolute doozy, with excellent weather once that moderate blow Friday abated. Congrats to all the winners, and congrats to Brandon from Queensland Fishing Classics and his support crew for a great job well done.

Hauling multiple fish up to the weighmaster is how you get yourself in the running for champion angler at the Woodgate Classic.

Junior winners from the Woodgate Beach Fishing Classic. Suss out the full list online.

Some of the senior category winners from the Woodgate Classic.

The rest of the senior category winners from the Woodgate Classic. Google the comp online for the full leader board results.

Burrum System in Shock from Last Weekend's Traffic

Word from folks fishing the Burrum system last weekend was of serious chaos as hordes of boaties roared up and down the four rivers to catch winners for the Woodgate Beach Hotel Fishing Classic. Some found the fishing that bit tougher because of the traffic, whilst others were lucky enough to score their desired target species with enough effort.

Given the inherent river clarity and time of year, it should be no surprise that there are mackerel within the river mouth. Schoolies have been most consistent, but there was at least one spaniard caught from the pontoon as well. Tailor could be expected over this full moon period, offering perhaps the last of the best of their run for another season.

The one standout species that bit particularly well during last weekend's neaps was the mighty mangrove jack. There were some rippers weighed-in at the Woodgate comp, and no doubt plenty more caught by river regulars. Nothing like clean water in a bait-rich river and a spike in temperature to fire up the local red dogs. Chase them again this weekend if you like. It may not be as warm, but it is decidedly warmer than a month ago, so they will relish a full moon feeding spree no doubt.

The Burrum's barra and threadfin salmon are being pestered relentlessly by a growing fleet of livescope-armed fishos bouncing from one hotspot to the next. Reacting to the lack of action and moving on when you suspect others have tampered with 'your' schools of fish has been a necessity to keep the bites coming. The full moon will be more challenging for all and sundry, so be prepared to consider alternatives such as the flats and species other than the apex predators when the tide is roaring.

CJ Higgins scored top junior honours at Woodgate. This young gun features regularly in local comp winner lists.

How's this for a memorable capture from the Burrum Heads boat ramp pontoon!

Prawn imitations make catching threadies like this one of Stuart's quite easy.

Tarj Wilson bettered his PB grunter with this fine creek specimen recently.

Barra and Threadies Turn it On in the Mary

River regulars are experiencing similar frustrations on the mighty Mary River system as enhanced traffic means a race for hotspots at the same time as the modern-day lack of etiquette impacts one's ability to fish a spot in peace. There was nowhere near the traffic on the Mary as was on the Burrum last weekend, but it was still hectic. The fog didn't help much either, creating its own issues for those trying to travel at speed or during the wee hours.

All the same, some very impressive barramundi and threadfin salmon were caught. Some crews caught multiple, whilst others didn't. Repeat efforts in the same spots this weekend will be beyond challenging as the bigger full moon tides roar up and down the river. Those in the know will adjust and target fish corralling fodder on the flats or in bodies of water not as adversely-affected by current flow.

Others will cleverly shift their focus to whiting on the flood tide and flathead on the ebb in the lower reaches. Others will target grunter mooching upriver with the tide, whilst some may simply target mackerel, bream, blues, jews and cod around the heads.

The Great Sandy Straits beckons for savvy estuary fishos keen to get the most from the full moon tides. Barra and threadies are decidedly easier targets down that way, and share those waters with plenty of blue salmon and a growing population of grunter. Jewies are a good target for nocturnal activities over along Fraser's western ledges, whilst mackerel, trevally and lots of queenfish are doing the rounds through the channels and around the islands.

Whiting fans will be eyeing the weather for another crack at the 'ting this full moon. You could join them for an early evening flood tide session after pumping a supply of yabbies over the afternoon low tide if you wish. Bag limits are a pretty easy affair in the right spots on these tides, and there are ample grounds fringing Fraser's western shores, the bay islands and down the straits that you can try.

Take the kids for a sight-fishing session chasing flathead if you prefer. There are seemingly endless locations that could have flathead ambush spot written all over them, but only so many that support the motherlode. Find flats and creeks draining into channels and you are already in the game. Highly-pressured waters like ours see a lot of boats in good weather, so be mobile and keep on the hunt if at first you do not succeed. There are stacks of flatties about, and they will bite well this week.

Ray was one of many to score red emperor last weekend.

Ray headed wide and scored a nice feed of mixed reefies.

School reds bit well offshore last weekend, along with plenty of other reefies.

Scott Welch put his new Ocean's Legacy PE 2 Focal to the test and it performed admirably.

Mackerel Moving in While Snapper Moving Out

Better weather will see the southern bay roar to life again as countless boats charge about looking for some fun or a feed. Some might pick up a late season snapper over these full moon tides, if they can avoid the relentless scourge of the sharks. Otherwise, it will be a matter of finding some squire, grassy sweetlip, or maybe a nannygai, then focussing your efforts on cod and trout at the turn of tide. Trout on the shallow reefs are a springtime special that could be an option for trollers and others on these tides too.

If that is all too much of a challenge, then mackerel might be appealing. There were broadies to be caught off Gatakers Bay last weekend, so there will be some of that clan elsewhere this week. The schoolies aren't too hard to find off Gatakers and off the Burrum, with increasing numbers appearing in our local shipping channels now too.

Tourists fishing the bay for the first time could keep it ultra-simple and go beacon-bashing this full moon. Baitfish gathered to shelter around the Fairway, the NU2 and its nearby shipwreck attract pelagics including mackerel, as do other less popular beacons. Drift by while you spin flat-out with a Flasha spoon, perform a drive-by trolling divers or park-up for a live-baiting session. One way or the other, you could be smoking or frying mackerel for dinner that night.

Try the bay islands for queenfish and trevally if the kids are up to a little casting fun. Trolling for marlin up in the northern pocket of Platypus Bay could appeal to some, even though there was possibly only the one fish caught last weekend. The mackerel and tuna broke the monotony for those crews that made some effort on the billies, so you could haul your kids up that way for some pelagic action.

Talk of a show of striped marlin offshore east of Fraser last week has stirred the heavy tackle fleet into early action. Those stripes were fish around the 200lb mark, so whilst not the big blues or blacks that the heavy tackle guys are so keen on, they are impressive fish and worthy opponents all the same. There are very interesting times ahead for the local game fishing fleet, particularly as the next new moon draws nearer.

Take advantage of better weather come Sunday or Monday and you can try the central and northern bay for reef fish. Snapper would be a great chance from the likes of the 25 Fathom Hole and surrounding hotspots, as well as at The Gutters. Same goes for the grounds off Wathumba, Station Hill and Rooneys Point, as snapper schools ready to migrate back offshore fill their bellies in readiness for the journey.

There are simple things you can do with the family 'up the island', such as chase fish around the coffee rock dotted along the Platypus Bay beaches, chase whiting along the same beaches (or better still, within Wathumba Creek) or go searching for surface action when not enjoying the obligatory whale-watching. Go hunt the mixed trevally clans lurking around the deeper reefs and massive bait schools up that way, and look out for huge cobia while you are there. Pick your weather and a great time and some delicious fresh seafood is assured.

Good luck out there y'all …… Jase

It's a school holiday fishing comp bonanza again this year. Get the kids involved at Toogoom next weekend.

Join the fun at the Toogoom Fishing Club's annual competition next weekend. Lots of great fishing tackle prizes supplied by Fishos once again.

entry.title: Fisho's Weekly Fishing Report – 18th September, 2026
entry.content:
Fisho's staffer and supposed Urangan Pier tuna guru Kealan Peaker with the result of his latest efforts.

Awesome Early Springtime Weather

With the vigorous south-easterly change and yesterday's strong wind warning out of the way, the week ahead is looking particularly appealing for Fraser Coast fishos. Sunny skies and a building northerly breeze will warm things up again whilst remaining ultra-pleasant for one and all.
