This morning's 20-knot south-easter is scheduled to ease gradually, and should leave us with 10-15 knots by lunchtime. Glorious conditions will greet boaties heading out early Saturday. A light and variable zephyr will barely ruffle the bay's surface until the northerly kicks in inshore during the late afternoon.

A prevailing northerly sea breeze Saturday evening will leave a little residual jiggle on the bay that early risers will experience Sunday morning, but it too is another great day with barely 10 knots from the north after a calmer morning. Being neap tides, the bay's currents won't exaggerate wave action so much, but you will face wind-against-tide for the first few hours of daylight.

The weekend weather sets the stage for the first of the working week, with basically light to no breeze early then a sea breeze each afternoon. A more defined onshore easterly seems likely by mid-week, when a stray shower or two may grace our coastline. More good weather thereafter could see the first week of the September school holidays be rather exhausting for fishing-mad kids and their just-as-keen parents.

The set of neap tides around this Saturday's first quarter phase half-moon are particularly relaxed, meaning minimal tidal flow throughout the weekend. Excellent tides for so many piscatorial pursuits, and our fish's mobility and enthusiasm for a feed will only grow with the making tides thereafter.

C'mon Dane, you can't count tiddlers like that in your daily tally at Monduran.

That's more like it Dane. Average Mondy barra are big and fat and they sure love those Jig Flies.

Activity Spikes at Urangan Pier

A significant biomass of baitfish are well-entrenched beneath Urangan Pier at present, and unlikely to go anywhere anytime soon. Masses of herring (and other baitfish) are having an increasingly hard time trying to shelter from the onslaught of passing pelagic predators, as well as plenty that have taken up temporary residence.

Building in numbers over the past week or so have been school mackerel in ever-improving size classes. There are still undersized juvies that need to be returned, but for the most part, catching a mackerel for dinner shouldn't be too hard. The usual Flasha spoons as well as alternative metal slugs are the favoured way of tempting mackerel for most kids and many adult pier regulars. Gang-rigged live herring being the alternative for those with less energy to burn.

Joining the mackerel this past week has been a wave or two of giant trevally, and a few golden trevally as well. Queenies are yet to show up (but they will when the whiting get extra thick), and only one spanish mackerel has been caught this week. Broad-barred mackerel can be expected to make an appearance sometime soon, adding even more appeal to the pier fishery for mackerel fans.

Longtail tuna were caught by some of the regulars whilst the tides were right over the past week. Timing can be everything when it comes to intercepting these speedsters, but the capture itself can be fairly simple. Should there be return runs of tuna while the pier is packed shoulder to shoulder with kids out the deep end, then some fancy footwork and quick reflexes will be required to avoid tangles and bust-offs.

Flathead provide a very appealing target for sight-fishing in the first channel and along the slope nearer the deep end. The water remains clear enough to spot them, so learn to be sneaky when you do, or someone noticing you noticing the flathead may well beat you back to the fish with a live bait. Secure a pike in lieu of herring and you will have the edge on your neighbours in the flathead department by the way.

All this pelagic action accompanying the abundance of baitfish can be a drawcard for sharks in warming waters. Add the motza of discarded baitfish etc and you can imagine just how the last 70 metres or so of the pier becomes one big oversized 'berley pot'. Needless to say, there will be hopefuls vying for jaws during the dark hours these holidays, and very likely plenty more thereafter.

Jig flies are all the rage for modern-day livescopers chasing impoundment barra.

Terry Allwood from Flick It Charters back in his element at Mondy catching barra.

Sand Whiting Have Arrived Along Our Town Beaches

After a fairly insignificant showing late August into spring, we can now confirm the arrival of schools of sand whiting along our north-facing town beaches and beneath Urangan Pier. These neap tides are hardly conducive to a good bite, so you might be watching schools swim by from aloft rather than catching them for a few days, but things are looking great on the whiting front come the full moon.

Once the tides build, say mid-week or so, there will be sufficient flow in the tide to get the whiting feeding. With water still so clear, night sessions will be most productive, yet daytime action can be triggered by the northerly breeze inbound very soon. Wave action creates turbulence that dislodges forage for the whiting whilst offering them a bit of cover in which they can sneak up into the shallows.

The stretch of beach we call Shelly Beach is very popular amongst local beach whiting fans. The groynes thereabouts offer a platform from which to target the 'ting too. Family fishos trying to keep sane and minimise sand intrusion in their littl'n's tackle etc can take advantage of the storm water pipes that traverse the beach at Torquay and expect plenty of action from whiting as well as passing dart and small bream.

The run of whiting at present is of a fairly average class of fish, yet those putting in some effort after dark have been rewarded with a very good feed. Better-quality whiting can be expected to turn up with the full moon tides. All good news for the folks from Hervey Bay Amateur Fishing Club who will be hosting their annual Junior Whiting Fishing Comp Saturday-week, and for all the kids bound to enjoy that fun day out.

A bag limit of whiting is on the cards as the full moon draws closer. There are stacks in the straits and they are now cruising our town beaches as well.

Beau Muscat's big cobia ate a live yakka and proceeded to give him the customary workout.

Woodgate Beach Fishing Classic is Underway

Very likely the folks having the most fun this weekend will be those involved in the ultra-popular Woodgate Beach Fishing Classic. Boasting more than $200,000 in prizes and giveaways, this year's event is already bigger and better than ever.

The weather isn't perfect, but it is still very good, so some pretty impressive fish can be expected to grace the weighmaster's tables this year. With our rivers in prime condition, our beaches fishing well and plenty of fish to chase close inshore, competitors without the big offshore rigs will have ample opportunity to compete with those heading out wider. The weather today will be a leveller, then it will be on for young and old.

Suss out all the details and the expansive list of eligible species by googling the event online. You can still enter if you haven't already done so, and your entry alone is enough to see you in the draw for a $75,000 Ford Ranger. Check out all the other wondrous prizes and giveaways on offer, and you are bound to be tempted to join the fun this weekend.

Being a family-focussed comp, your kids will be assured a great time, and won't stand a chance of being bored at any time. Given that the comp is run from the Woodgate Beach Hotel, you won't go thirsty or hungry, but you might struggle with early starts the mornings after the nightly escapades.

Good luck to all competitors this weekend. We will bring you a wrap-up of the event next week, but you can watch it all unfold via the comp's Live Leader Board online if you like. It will be Toogoom Fishing Club's turn to host their comp the week after, so why not back-up your weekend at Woodgate with another wonderful weekend of fun and games these school holidays.

Need a new tinny. Just enter the Woodgate Beach Hotel Fishing Classic and you are one step closer to winning one of these beauties.

Get lucky enough at the Woodgate Beach Fishing Classic and you could be launching this rig at the ramp next weekend.

Merch galore is on offer for entrants in the Woodgate Beach Hotel Fishing Classic this weekend.

Woodgate Beach Hotel grounds swelling with prizes, stage and exhibits ready for the big event.

Head Wide Over the Neap Tides if You can

The weather on offer for offshore boaties this weekend is actually better than what inshore boaties can expect. Suss out the wind forecasts for Sandy Cape and you will see what I mean. There is a spike in swell and sea due to the blow that arrived late Wednesday, but conditions will be vastly improved by Saturday.

The typical springtime scenario is unfolding; whereby a northerly sea breeze created by the difference between the cooler sea and a warming land mass only impacts waters closer inshore. In essence, the wider you get from land, the lighter the breeze.

It can be a jiggly old trip up the bay for the first hour or so, but if you, your crew and your vessel are truly offshore capable, then that should not phase you one bit. Once out there, bounce around looking for fish across the Sandy Cape Shoals, along the cusp of the continental shelf east of there or maybe even wider along the continental slope if you are sporting deep drop tackle.

Expect plenty of variety in your reef fish haul once offshore east of Breaksea Spit. Joining the expansive list of possible tropical reef species out there are snapper and pearlies that are still moving further offshore and remain quite prolific in waters this side of the shelf (for now). Head more north than east and end up beyond the light-ship towards Lady Elliott and it might be some pretty impressive reds gracing your esky for the long haul home.

Wander across to the Gutters and you can catch a good feed, so long as you keep mobile if the sharks find you. Coral trout are likely for those hopping the usual prawn imitation softies or live baiting, with the ever-likely bycatch of estuary cod and with any luck, a nice nanny or two. Expect plenty of action from grassy sweetlip and other 'sweetlips' and 'perches', and maybe a little snapper action come dawn, dusk or during the evening.

Whilst neap tides won't excite any experienced bay snapper fishos, the 25 Fathom Hole and grounds in that central bay area can still produce during periods of low light. You might've missed your best opportunity for snapper over Wathumba way last weekend, but there will still be fish there somewhere.

The whales are 'bad' out in the bay, and also quite the hazard close inshore. Recent stories of whales popping up within cooee of Urangan Harbour, Gatakers Bay and near the bay islands should be noted, as our waters are still alive with serious numbers of these wondrous leviathans. Offshore fishos need to be extra-wary, not just due to the possible numbers out there along the humpback highway, but also due to visibility issues created by even a subtle ground swell. Be wary folks, but enjoy every sighting as we all still do.

You won't forget the EPIRB again eh Matt. Two fish in two drops then sent home by Fisheries all the way from the Gutters - ouch!

Scotty would've loved to catch more trout like this one whilst at the Gutters briefly with Matt. Quiet trip home eh boys.

Mackerel Inshore and Trevally Aplenty Up the Bay

Wave after wave of school mackerel have been making their way into the bay for the past couple of weeks. There have been plenty off Gatakers Bay, Toogoom and the Burrum coast, and steadily increasing numbers in our shipping channels. The pros are hard at work in the western bay, but won't be trying their luck in the east until the whale numbers are 'acceptable'. So too, the sand crabbers. Commercial and recreational crabbers are resting their gear at present due to the unacceptably high risk of entanglement with our humpbacks.

Find a patch of reef in the northern bay that is alive with yakkas and other baitfish and there is a strong chance that there are trevally circling them waiting for their next trigger to feed. Hervey Bay's trevally population is quite impressive this time of year, and the variety of trevors making up that biomass is equally as impressive.

Take the kids for a jigging or softy-flicking session up in Platypus Bay and you can kick back and enjoy the fun and games as a variety of muscle-bound trevors thump away and get them huffing and puffing. There is tiny trevally up there and fully mature oversized brethren as well. Challenge your kids to see who can catch the greatest variety in a session and feel free to share the results, along with a few happy snaps, with us at Fishos.

You might spot schools of tuna feeding in your travels up that way. Most likely mac tuna from what we hear, but stray larger longtails are still a chance. Be prepared for encounters with monster cobia too, as these big old brutes have been doing the rounds in the bay for months.

Talk of Hervey Bay marlin has been minimal of late, yet there are small blacks out there for anyone keen to try their hand. One free-jumper seemingly unhappy with the contents of its throat was witnessed going nuts by whale-watchers this week. Maybe the 15-20 kilo juvie ate something it shouldn't have. They do tend to throw caution to the wind and mouth all sorts of potential tucker at that age it seems.

Those of you that have been around these parts long enough will recall the fantastic runs of sailfish that used to impress all and sundry eons ago. Many of those captures were at this time of year, from the grounds north of Rooneys as well as offshore off the 13 Mile and Spit Bommie. The return of slimy mackerel to Hervey Bay waters this winter may be a drawcard to see a return of the sails. Who knows? Only those that go looking for them will know for sure.

Regardless of whether the sails return or not, there is bound to be some extra effort on the baby black marlin light tackle scene in coming weeks and months. As is typical, most folks will wait until they hear of numbers being caught before they join the fray. This might be a September to remember for those willing to put in the effort ahead of the crowds. Winter's bay marlin fishing was the best seen for many a year after all.

Lou caught this fine grunter from the Booral Flats shore-based not that long ago.

Keep an eye out for tuna like this longtail of Kingy Ridgeway's in your travels up the bay.

Not a Weekend to Miss if you Relish Catching Barra and Sambos

You had a chance to enjoy A-grade river fishing two weeks ago when the tides and a spike in temperatures combined to produce a memorable bite from our barra and salmon. This weekend is every bit as good, if not better, and promises great things for all who work the tides and time their assaults correctly.

Choose to wander the mighty Mary chasing trophy barra and monster threadies if you like. Should your ego need no more massaging, then settle back on numbers of fish gathered around snags, eddies and ambush locations and catch what is a very healthy class of fish right now.

The waters are too clear for the remaining gillnetters that still work the Mary system to operate over these tides, so go your hardest with an array of large prawn imitations, suspending hardbodies and some soft vibes or paddle-tails for the barra, and mix it up with smaller versions of the same for the threadies. You may or may not find the motherlode, but you are bound to find at least some fish, and they are highly likely to be very active and on the chew.

Bycatch, or potential targets in their own, might include blue salmon, estuary cod and grunter, as well as maybe a decent jewfish or two amongst the undersized models that hug some of the snags, deep holes and rock bars. Stay downstream to mix it with a few flathead, and return for more of them plus whiting and bream when the full moon tides draw nearer.

There are very good hauls of whiting to be caught in the lower Susan as well as the lower Mary at least as far up as the Crab Islands. Popular hangouts are the channels and verges between the sandbanks, all of which aren't far from a source of fresh yabbies. Like I said though, wait for better tides for a serious crack at the 'ting.

Hit the Burrum instead and join the crowd from the Woodgate comp and you could be jostling for position on any number of barramundi schools. There are plenty of threadies to catch up there too, even though they may not rival the Mary's fish in the size stakes. Add the very real chance of emerging mangrove jacks though, and the Burrum system certainly has its own appeal.

Big whiting in the Gregory and the lower-mid Burrum will join quality grunter on the chew when the full moon glows brighter. Bream numbers are better than they have been in years up there if they take your fancy, and there are still numbers of flathead available for those that have worked out that they need to poke a little further upstream.

The local creek and river mud crabbing continues to impress many folks that keep putting in the effort. Clearer saline waters have marched them well upstream, and they are frequenting backwaters, gullies and barely accessible hideaways more-so than the open stretches of recent months. Notwithstanding, they are still potting well, even for this time of year. If you don't want to waste precious 'barra time' on crabs this weekend, then consider dropping the pots in over the coming full moon instead.

Scotty from Focussed Fishing and Fisho's with proof you can catch monster threadies after dark on lures.

That's not a tuna Kealan! Tasty rods those Samurais eh mate.

Sí, Señor – See You on Fraser

Whilst Wednesday's south-easterly change and the prevailing breeze since then has made for very challenging surf fishing conditions, there is still some rather impressive fishing to look forward to as soon as the seas settle. School holiday crowds will be disembarking the barges in droves for the next fortnight, and the island's surf beaches will be rather hectic. So too could the fishing be potentially.

Possibly the best run of tailor so far this season was enjoyed by a number of crews camping in the central sector of the island. Patrons of Fraser Island Retreat at Happy Valley in particular have been doing very well, and they haven't been driving too far to find the fish. Quality tailor in the 50-55cm size range have been a welcome improvement on the largely barely legal choppers earlier this season.

Dart have been of particularly good size in the same area, offering excellent sport and a surprisingly tasty meal for those swapping gang-rigged pilchards for more appropriate pippies, whitebait, froggies and/or pilchard pieces. No word of jewies over the recent darks, though that is not to say there weren't any caught. Whiting do remain a challenge in the central sector, so maybe they will improve with the full moon.

Most impressive of all, has been the excellent run of spanish mackerel that have been raiding the surf gutters. On the hunt for tailor, some of these spaniards are real whoppers in the 20-kilo class, that put on a great show on surf tackle heavy enough to subdue them. Whilst mostly the domain of drone fishos and slide-baiters who can get their baits to the second gutter beyond the surf break, you too have the option to try for a spaniard with your heaviest tailor rod if you wish to try.

Simply catch a tailor of legal size, and not too big. Remove your hooks from its gob and pin it in the back midway to its tail by the trailing hook of a set of 7/0 gang hooks on a heavy mono leader (or an 8/0 single hook on single-strand wire) with no sinker in the mix. Return the well-cared-for tailor to a gutter draining to sea via a rip and give it free line to swim back out. Best if said gutter isn't frequented by other fishos, and even better if the rip is a feeder to the second gutter beyond the sandbanks breaking the waves. Not suitable in big onshore seas, in crowds, or if there are too many sharks about, obviously.

It won't be long (1st October) and you can try for spaniards from the rocks at the headlands once the season opens. No doubt plenty of keen tailor fishos will be there tossing stickbaits and slugs for tailor, so why not up the ante and toss larger stickies more suited to attracting a spaniard. You never know, the mother of all tailor might take a liking to the same large stickbait too.

GTs are a surf zone possibility as well this season. They have been crash tackling live baits set for spaniards down off Double Island Point and Rainbow Beach just this week. Spanish mackerel have been active down there too. Surf fishing for whopper speedsters is steadily becoming a major pastime for tuned-in fishos willing to test their skills on the sand. Joining them is an ever-increasing number of folks intent on tangling with sharks in the surf zone, whilst all and sundry get to interact with the noahs when live baiting with tailor at some time, like it or not.

Good luck out there y'all …… Jase

It's a school holiday fishing comp bonanza again this year. Get the kids involved at Toogoom next weekend.

Join the fun at the Toogoom Fishing Club's annual competition next weekend. Lots of great fishing tackle prizes supplied by Fishos once again.

entry.title: Fisho's Weekly Fishing Report – 11th September, 2026
entry.content:
Leo Arnold has already caught some impressive reef fish at the ripe old age of 6. A true young gun in the making.

Substantially Cooler This Week

Following a memorably warm kickstart to spring last week, yesterday's rather cool change felt downright chilly. A subtle spike in local water temperatures was recorded prior to this change but those numbers are unlikely to rise this week.

The south-easter peaked at 25 knots in the bay late yesterday, and maybe 30 knots offshore. Strong wind warning status was only declared briefly and is now cancelled. Today's 20 knotter will ease slightly for the weekend. Scattered showers riding 15-20 knot winds Saturday and 15 knots Sunday pretty much sums up the weekend ahead. A brief window of calm seas Tuesday prior to the arrival of another blustery change mid-week offers your best chance of heading for open waters.

It's a new moon today, so strong tidal flow is a given for a couple more days to come before the tidal variation plunges. Mid-afternoon low tides and extra-dark nights appeal to many marine creatures this time of year. Spawning activity will peak for some if it hasn't already. A great bite could be anticipated from reef fish, pelagics and our flats-favouring estuarine species. The weather isn't ideal, yet great fishing is in the offing for those willing to take on the breeze.

Jack was one of many fishos to get amongst the salties last weekend.

Ryan enjoyed success on our local salties when temperatures spiked last week.

Urangan Pier Fishing About to Get Better

Masses of greenback herring have been seeking refuge beneath Urangan Pier for the past week or two. They are large herring, making appealing fodder for passing pelagic predators. One such critter that is highly sought after by pier-goers is the longtail tuna. Favourable tides should see a few caught if they are foolish enough to come within casting range of the pier this weekend.

School mackerel are entertaining plenty of folks out at the deep end at the moment too. Small fish generally, with some undersized and some making the grade. As always, it is a choice between spinning with spoons and live baiting with gang-rigged herring for most pier mackerel fans.

Another technique used decades ago when even your scribe frequented the planks, was to fashion a belly strip bait from a herring and pin it at the tip of one end on a single o'shaughnessy hook. The belly strip being cut from throat latch to bum hole, creating what could be described as a little 'canoe'.

Wogged against the tide mid-water column 70cm behind an appropriate-sized sinker resting on a swivel, this neat flashy silver little belly strip has been the undoing of many schoolies and broadies when they seem resistant to other offerings. A handy alternative in GT season when catching schoolies for live baits actually warranted some effort by those of us otherwise uninterested in the toothy critters.

Schoolies are bound to be a major drawcard for holidaying school kids come the September holidays. The pier is quite often at its very best during this particular school break, when mackerel and other pelagics join whiting, flathead and a few other randoms creating entertainment overload for the kids.

Flathead captures have been mentioned this past week, with the recent neaps being notably productive, as they should be. Bream numbers have tapered off, but you could still catch a few remnant fish over the new moon. Better to shift your focus to whiting to be honest though, and be ready for when they front-up at the pier.

Riley McLeod's photogenic big diamond trevally prior to release.

Brett got amongst the barra at Monduran like many others during the recent warm spell.

6th Annual Junior Whiting Fishing Comp Just Two Weeks Away

A spell of northerly winds over last week's neap tides was a timely occurrence, as that breeze triggered migratory movements from our local sand whiting. No word of serious numbers along our town beaches as yet, but they won't be far away. There are stacks over Moon Point way and plenty elsewhere locally. Coming weeks will see crowds gather as the whiting move in along the Torquay-Urangan beachscape and beneath the pier.

The local whiting run should be just hitting its straps when the Junior Whiting Fishing Competition is hosted by the good folks from the Hervey Bay Amateur Fishing Club later this month. The event is exceptionally well-timed and well-positioned, being held the day before the full moon, at Lower Dayman Park in Urangan.

Kicking off at 7.30am Saturday 26th September, this very popular event will see oodles of kids roll up for lots of fun and frivolities. Swags of prizes are on offer, donated to the club by Fisho's Tackle World. Competing in 3 age groups; under 8's, under 12's and under 16's; the kids are bound to have a ball and stand a very even chance of sharing in the prizes and the glory.

All kids must be accompanied by an adult at all times, and should arrive at the comp donning sunscreen and a hat. Bring them armed with their own fishing rod and reel, some terminal tackle, a bucket and their bait. Yabbies will be second only to live blood worms for bait for those that can access same, whilst cured beach worms from Fisho's will serve nicely as a convenient alternative for those keeping it simple.

Onsite cast net demonstrations are bound to educate the youngsters, where their participation will be encouraged if they are inclined to have a go. A free sausage sizzle at 11am will see an end to the fishing, followed by the prize presentations. Call 0493 065 729 to register your children and watch the hype build as the day nears. Fun times for all involved come the 26th no doubt.

Fraser Guided Fishing clients get to enjoy the pleasures of flathead fishing as well as chasing pelagics and reefies this time of year.

Aedan Arnold and crew headed for 1770 last weekend and brought home some quality reef fish.

Mackerel Arrive Inshore

Word is that commercial netters have commenced catching school mackerel in the south-western bay. The usual grounds off the Burrum and off Toogoom have been where the effort has been focussed to date. Wave after wave of mackerel are expected to pass through those and other local waters as the inshore biomass builds in coming weeks.

The size class of the mackerel will improve with time too. Right now, there are plenty of pesky little undersized models in the mix, so it can pay to bounce from school to school to find the better-quality fish. Fans of trolling tactics can cover ground quickly if not forever stopping to retrieve the mackerel. As always, there will be those that like to spin for them with spoons, those that favour live baits and those that deploy the simple gang-rigged pilly. All will catch mackerel at some time.

Hot on the tails of these lesser mackerel will be a wave or two of spaniards. Bigger spanish mackerel tend to predate on the schoolies and will follow select schools. GTs will scoff mackerel with vigour too when they arrive later in spring. Having said that, there has already been a couple of unseasonal large GT captures close inshore, so who knows, there might be an earlier run this year.

Schoolies have also been a feature of the River Heads fishery of late, where both boaties and land-based fishos can spin them up on spoons of simply target them with baits. Given the prevalence of herring in the river mouth and surrounds, it should be obvious what bait is appropriate. Broad-barred mackerel are also possible from the River Heads area, as well as further down the straits.

Tarj Costigan's 1st Mondy barra went 102cm. A PB that probably won't last long this season.

Rhys Costigan scored a new PB barra at Lake Monduran measuring a mighty 117cm on the mat.

Tales Of Snapper, Weed, Whales and False Killers

Algal blooms and an annoying presence of snot weed was mentioned in last week's report. Without going into nearly so much detail, word is that the snotty stuff is still impacting open waters of the bay. Its negative impact is mostly due to its tendency to gather on your line and/or lure, but the waters remain fishable. Suffice to say, we all wish this weed an immediate bon voyage and hope it doesn't spread further inshore.

Whale watchers have been revelling in the ever-growing numbers of humpbacks dropping in to rest in our waters during their return journey south. Adding to the whale watching highlights have been the presence of around 40 false killer whales in Platypus Bay waters recently, along with at least one Bryde's Whale.

This is all fantastic for we nature lovers, and we all certainly love our whales, yet boaties seem more nervous than ever at the same time. As you can imagine, more and more skippers are even deferring repeats of past traditional trips to Platypus Bay for night-time sojourns on the snapper and the like, and northern bay fishos are keener to overnight it up north than to drive home in the dark of night.

Opportunities missed perhaps, as these tides over the dark of this new moon, are traditionally highly productive ones for Hervey Bay snapper fishing. The many grounds off Rooneys, Station Hill, Wathumba and further south in Platypus Bay would normally host numbers of snapper gathered to feast on the baitfish abundance post-spawn prior to their return journey offshore some time soon.

Ample opportunity exists to tangle with knobbies on soft plastics and jigs during daylight hours (as well as after dark). Whilst bait fishos gather their livies and recently deceased versions of the same yakkas etc during daylight in readiness for dusk-into-evening sessions on anchor over favoured grounds. Subtle yet consistent berley trails assured an anchored snapper fisho of success once upon a time, but it would seem somewhat foolhardy today with so many sharks about.

If your vessel and crew can handle the prevailing south-easter up the island, where its inherent protective nature dampens the breeze dramatically, then snapper success might be an option this weekend. Larger vessels sporting keen enough crew could even take on the more open waters of the bay comfortably in 15 knots or less. Out there you will find snapper just as eager to bite, and probably even easier to find.

Sean found some of the yellowtail kingfish cruising our waters. They will disappear once things warm up further.

Terry Allwood with one of two big Hervey Bay cobia caught on Fly Jigs he uses to catch barra at Mondy.

Your Should've Been There Last Week

If you didn't make the effort to go barra fishing, or at least chase some other estuarine predators last week while the warm north wind blew, then you missed out – big time! Conditions and tides were highly favourable, and some very fine barramundi and threadfin salmon were caught. There is plenty of fish in our rivers right now, so don't miss the next opportunity like that one should it arise.

Big new moon tides and a chill in the wind combine to make this weekend vastly less appealing to regular barra fishos, yet some will have a crack regardless. Such is the extra appeal that livescope and the like have made for those sporting such high tech. The Great Sandy Straits will be a better default option for those keen to try their hand this weekend all the same.

The flats fishery down the straits can be very appealing, particularly given the sight-fishing opportunities in what will be the clearest water we will see for some time. You could keep it simple and kick back catching another bag limit of whiting, or a swag of flathead if you like. You could go chase queenfish for fun, and very likely enjoy bycatch such as trevally and maybe some blue salmon.

Hit the creeks of the straits and look for schools of barra, roaming threadies, or packs of jacks parked up in the snags. Hop some smaller soft plastic prawns through the creek channels or the feeder channels beyond and see if the grunter have returned as yet. Opt for a session chasing jewfish along Fraser's western ledges if that appeals, or go trolling along the same ledge frontages to see how many cod you can catch in a session. Spoilt for choice you are. Go you should, young Jedi.

Jacko's latest jewfish capture, aided by his Lowrance Active Target set-up.

Even a flathead fisho can catch threadfin salmon this time of year, eh Jacko.

Gutters Galore on Fraser's Surf Beaches

Word from locals on Fraser's surf-side suggests the fishing has been a little challenging on the tailor and whiting fronts, but other species have been making up for them. There was a good tailor bite a week ago when the low tides coincided with sunset. Select gutters in the central sector of the island fished well as soon as the sun dipped below the cliffs or dunes behind the beach and it was easy to score a feed of modest choppers. Since then, it has been tougher, and this south-easter isn't helping those over there right now.

Very good quality dart have been caught regularly in the same central sector of the island, south of the headlands. Taking pilly baits and sometimes even lures, the dart are better targeted with pippies if you are keen to score them in numbers. Dart fight harder than most other beach dwellers by the way, and taste better than tailor fresh for many palates.

Flathead have been lurking on the fringes of some gutters and at the corners where melon holes escape to sea. Rarely fussy, the flatties will scoff a pippy or a pilly just as keenly, and could be a fun option for those tossing appropriately-weighted softies about in the surf zone. Whiting numbers have not been great in the middle of the island apparently, yet there are still sufficient fish there to warrant some effort over the new moon tides.

Jewfish hunters will probably be cursing this wind arriving when it did. The peaking dark of the moon tides having jewfish-catching history on the island. Pippies have been easy enough to find lately. Wormers are doing it a bit tough though. Shifting sands caused by unseasonal onshore blows over winter didn't help on that front. The island's headlands remain closed to all forms of fishing and gathering, so don't be tempted to fish within 400m of Waddy or Indian in any direction.

The opening of that closure can't come fast enough for some fishos keen to go spinning from the rocks. In the meantime, some pretty impressive spanish mackerel are being caught from deeper tailor-filled gutters north and south of the headlands. Drone fishos are catching 20 kilo+ spaniards apparently, so one would assume a few slide baiters would be keen to get in on that action too.

A notably increased number of shark fishos are on the island at the moment. Some of those droning out live baits aren't necessarily targeting spaniards it seems. Given Fraser's abundant shark population you would assume those guys don't have to wait long for a bite. Their crews watching on might have a while to wait though, as some of the noahs cruising Fraser's surf gutters are sizeable. Hence the reason no-one surfs or swims beyond the shallows on Fraser.

Travel wise, the island is quite appealing, even though the sand is drying and softening for high tide travel. The rocks are exposed at Yidney and Poyungan, but both sets are passable at low tide. High tide passage is denied, so It's over and around for all who time it wrong. Resorts in the central sector have mentioned the prevalence of late arrivals lately (often after dark), as folks timed their run up the beach all wrong.

Eli Creek itself is a major issue for beach travellers, as a high bank with a metre drop on the north side limits passage beyond to 3 hours either side of low tide. The beach is very busy again, so crowds are to be expected at this and many other popular tourist attractions. Happy Valley residents and visitors will be glad to learn that the ramp access that is currently only one lane with stop/go lights will be reopened to two lanes for the upcoming school holidays.

Be a part of the fun-loving crowd at this year's Woodgate Beach Fishing Classic.

Your kids will have an absolute ball at the Woodgate Beach Fishing Classic, particularly during the big Kids Day Out event on Saturday.

Woodgate Beach Fishing Classic is On Next Weekend

It's back for year number 10, and promising to be bigger and better than ever. The Woodgate Beach Fishing Classic is on again and it's a must-attend event on the local fishing competition calendar and an incredible social event in its own right. If you haven't already done so, book your family and/or friends in for a fat time starting next Friday 18th September for 3 days solid of fishing and fun galore.

As if the fishing itself, plus the whopping $200,000+ in prizes and giveaways wasn't enough, this year's event is sporting some very impressive activities to keep you and the fam entertained to the max. The Shimano Fishing Simulator will be onsite, displayed on a massive TV screen for all to view. The Best Dressed Team comp itself promises to be a hoot, and you can even book a ride in a helicopter for a mere $65.

Dane from Fisho's will be in attendance to help with fishing clinics for the kids and will be there to hand out the $21,000+ in fishing category prizes supplied and/or donated by Fisho's. The kids will be spoilt rotten during Saturday's Kids Day Out, with activities galore that include cart races, casting clinics and cast net throwing, followed by a cast-off casting competition. They will all sleep well that night!

Garmin's impressive onsite displays will have plenty of folks eyeing off their latest tech, whilst folks are doing the rounds selling raffle tickets that could see you add to your weekend's prize haul. There is a $75,000 ford Ranger up for grabs, just for registering in the comp. Anyone can win this beast, and the odds are great. Stacks of other lucky draw prizes for both kids and adults add to your chances of winning, and all this without even weighing in a fish.

There are limited tickets available for this one folks, so don't dilly dally or you could miss out! Jump online and google Woodgate Beach Fishing Classic to suss out the event program, expansive list of eligible species, the prizes on offer, and of course, to register for tickets. Ask anyone who has attended recent Woodgate Beach Classics and they will tell you; the Woodgate Beach Hotel is THE place to be 18th – 20th September 2026.

Good luck out there y'all …… Jase

Woodgate Classic

entry.title: Fisho's Weekly Fishing Report – 4th September, 2026
entry.content:
Terry and Cooper with the better trout from their mid-week Gutters session.

Smoking Hot Start to Spring

Concluding the mildest Fraser Coast winter this scribe can recall, the trend continues as spring kicks off with remarkably warm weather. Our inland neighbours will feel the warmth more than we will here within the influence of the northerly sea breeze, however, fine sunny days will appeal to all and sundry as we shake off yet another winter.

This morning's 10-15 knot north-wester should tend northerly later today, setting the trend for the weekend. Excellent and enjoyable conditions for all but open bay waters, where that prevailing northerly breeze will make things rather uncomfortable. Accept the facts and shift your focus to our estuaries or the sheltered waters of the straits and you will enjoy the 10-15 knot north-wester much more.

A dry south-easterly change appears likely to kick off the working week. No more than 15 knots initially, that drops out for a brief period early-mid week potentially. Much stiffer winds are forecast for later next week, that might bring some isolated showers to coastal parts. It might also create a proper bushfire risk if the wind really cranks after this warm drying spell. Don't be the instigator of such a catastrophe. Without lightning from storms to blame as the fire starters, there is only humans, so take extra care.

With the full moon well behind us now, our tides have been diminishing with the waning moon. Today's half moon commences the third quarter phase planting us smack-bang amongst another set of neaps. Great for estuarine activities, which is rather handy given the weather. There is much to be excited about this weekend if you are a keen pursuer of piscatorial predators in our rivers and creeks. No doubt many local dads will enjoy a ripper Father's Day come Sunday.

Cooper joined Dane and Tez for the day and took home some tasty morsels for future seafood banquets.

Coral trout were hard to tempt during a recent northern bay mission for Dane and crew. This one fell victim to a live bait.

Masses of Baitfish Dramatically Improve Pier Fishery

After months of having to deal with port-hole herring and a lesser biomass beneath Urangan Pier, the good news this week is that the greenbacks have returned – in force. Masses of more desirable herring means great things for the pier's pelagic fishery, and return for effort has already improved.

Queenfish have been a welcome returnee, joining numbers of undersized school mackerel to round up the hapless herring. A decent yellowtail kingfish was landed this week, from what has been a small school of sizeable kingies lurking there on and off recently. One spanish mackerel was also landed, whilst more could be anticipated if the baby schoolies they love to eat continue to linger.

Pier regulars tend to get excited about the proposition of hooking passing longtail tuna. Select tides improve their chances, as does a free-swimming herring tossed towards fish that come within casting range. Herring ballooned away from the pier can work too but this technique is wind and tide reliant. All basic stuff really, whilst not nearly as credit-worthy as the same fish tricked into munching on some form of artificial.

With bream "on their last legs" beneath the pier, it is the flathead in the shallows of the first channel or along the slope out beyond the sandbank that will catch a few pier fishos' attention over these neap tides. A nice distraction offering sight-fishing opportunities, whilst awaiting the whiting schools likely to turn up with these northerlies or thereafter during better tides.

Dane loves his seafood, no matter how it comes.

Kyro and Kingy Ridgeway were proud as punch with their lap full of longtail tuna.

Time to Dust off the Beach Whiting Tackle

Yes, that time of year is upon us, where northerly winds pummel our north-facing town beaches drawing whiting schools in close to feed. The tides may be poor right now, lacking run due to the current set of neaps, but the present conditions are excellent for creating a fun future fishery. Waters too clear for whiting to feed in during daylight will soon turn a little 'milkier'. Could this northerly trigger an early run of whiting feeding in the stirred-up waters? You will only know if you go have a crack.

Yabbies pinned to longshank hooks on ultra-light tackle sporting minimal sinker weight will be the whitings' undoing if they are there. Worms or peeled prawns making acceptable alternatives for those of you unable to pump yabbies. The latter stage of the rising tide is likely to be most productive, followed by the early stage of the ebb.

Much better whiting fishing can be anticipated closer to the next new moon in a week's time. A few days of northerly will have created the right 'soup' for the whiting to be drawn to, and the much bigger tides will trigger their feeding response. A better class of whiting will join their smaller brethren along our town beachscape, and the fringes beyond town will be worth trying too.

Those that would rather maximise the fun factor whilst catching shore-based whiting can put in some low tide effort with tiny topwater offerings on sharper-sloped beaches. Flatter terrain elsewhere being just as conducive at other times of tide. Trying to punch such ultra-light lures into a head-on breeze will be foolish, so choose your location/s based on the prevailing breeze. The Booral Flats offer excellent conditions should the north-wester dominate.

Eddie Whittle having a ball culling tilapia from his home lake. Well done son.

Kade Whittle can catch fish in a puddle. Doing his bit for our waterways by removing as many tilapia as possible.

Amberjack pull like the proverbial freight trains and are quite common on the shoals and the shelf east of Breaksea Spit.

Lukas was happy with this offshore kingy. Happy it wasn't any bigger most likely.

Algal Blooms Impact Hervey Bay Waters

Fraser Island surf fishos are rightly nervous about the potential impact of the dreaded snot weed in the island's surf gutters, yet in recent weeks, it has been the open waters of the northern bay that have been impacted. From Platypus Bay to the Southern Gutters, there is a suspended mess of snot weed playing havoc with both bait and lure fishos. Head further north and you will drive beyond the affected waters, so let's hope the prevailing northerlies don't push it further into the southern bay.

This snot weed is annoying because it gathers on your line, bulks-up on baits, hooks, jig heads and leader knots, all the while lessening your chances of a sneaky natural presentation. Thick enough weed accumulated can end up jamming up rod tips, guides and even laying a mess onto your reel. Did the unusually prevalent onshore winds this winter send it bay-bound? Not for me to surmise.

Also becoming more obvious, without the same negative effects, is the emergence of Trichodesmium (sometimes referred to as sea sawdust). Imagining a filamentous bacterium isn't as easy as an 'algal bloom', so that is what we tend to refer to this end-of-winter phenomenon as colloquially. Trichodesmium is highly beneficial to our nutrient-poor tropical waters, being the kick starter food source at the base of the food chain to a wonderful micro-organism biomass that so many creatures, including our piscatorial friends, rely on further up the food chain. This bloom will be with us for a few months to come.

A step up the very same food chain are the dinoflagellates that can be held responsible for the ciguatera toxin issues we have to live with in Platypus Bay waters. A bloom of these microbiomic life forms often occurs in October and directly impacts small demersal fishes and other creatures living in or above the substrate in Platypus Bay. Renowned for the worst ciguatera outbreaks known in Australia, this is why consuming certain predatory species that feed on select bottom-dwelling creatures in Platypus Bay is so risky that bans are in place. Case in point – spanish mackerel.

In a month or so's time, over the new moon period, there will be the annual coral spawning event that will see yet another stain of floating (and suspending) matter quite evident in the bay, offshore and right throughout the GBR. One more rung of our wondrous tropical waters food chain.

Nothing to be concerned about with any of the above, apart from some inconvenience with the snot weed perhaps. More likely to impact the inshore fishos, and particularly whiting fans fishing Fraser's western shores and the straits, is the red-brown algal weed that breaks away from its wintertime rocky hangouts with warming spring waters. Suss out future fishing grounds and if the 'weed' is an issue, then move elsewhere. Carried by the tides, you can still find spots free of this scourge and happily catch your next bag limit of 'ting. No word of this phenomenon at this stage by the way.

Massive estuary cod stretched Dane and crew prior to release when possible. This big old fish went back none the worse for wear.

Cod, cod and more cod. The big garbage-gutses were certainly on the chew mid-week out wide.

What would you rather do battle with Terry - Mondy barra or slimy old estuary cod.

Yellowfin tuna have turned up along the continental shelf. There will be more and bigger models to follow soon.

Lack of Life = Lack of Sharks

Good enough "bosses' weather" a couple of days ago saw a few crews head for the waters of the northern bay. Apart from the snot weed issue mentioned above, some found the going a bit tough on grounds at the Gutters that were remarkably devoid of "life". Sounder screens are expected to light-up with colourful interpretations of the fish below, yet on quite a few grounds otherwise known for accommodating ample reef fish and pelagics, there was very little to be seen.

The reef fish bite was quite sluggish accordingly, yet on the upside, the fish hooked were mostly hauled all the way to the boat without being taxed by sharks. Coral trout took live baits and lures, just in smaller numbers than hoped. Some decent-sized models were in the mix too, which may not have been landed at other times when the sharks are unbeatable.

The usual mix of other reef fish hit the deck, including venus tuskfish, squire, grassy sweetlip and nannygai. Just not that many of them in a pretty tough bite apparently. Making up for the lack of action from more desirable species though, were some rather large estuary cod. In fact, some grounds were lousy with chunky cod, and very little else.

Snapper were found at the 25 Fathom Hole, but again, only very few. Cobia were caught there and further north at the Gutters. Baitfish were prolific enough in the central bay, with yakkas leading the charge amongst a substantial mix of baitfish-types that included plenty of slimy mackerel. So, the baitfish are still out there, and good things can be expected on the snapper front on better tides around the new moon.

Offshore, there was a bit of action for those trolling the Sandy Cape Shoals and the nearby continental shelf. Spaniards were found over the shoal country, and yellowfin tuna on the shelf. At least one marlin was hooked and lost. Bound to be more of the same in coming months as hot water from up north pours down our way.

Red emperor were caught bottom-bashing, along with the usual mix of shoal dwellers such as venus tuskfish, red throat and other tasty reefies. Amberjack and yellowtail kingfish put the hurt on at least one crew, as bycatch whilst chasing reefies. Great jigging opponents if you are keen for a tussle. Flamies, pearlies and bar cod from the depths of the continental slope found their way to the surface attached to deep drop rigs.

Closer inshore, it has been challenging to beat the sharks at popular hotspots, yet a feed is possible for the mobile fisho. Snapper can still be expected this month, so try again if we get the weather come new moon time. Otherwise, try for coral trout on the deeper reefs and expect some estuary cod bycatch. It won't be long and the shallow reef coral trout fishery will come online. The new moon in October would be a prime time to be prepared for them if not before.

Mention of winter whiting off Gatakers Bay was heard last week. Northerlies will put paid to that option until the winds drop or return to southerly origins. There should be ample winteries elsewhere close to shore too, from the grounds west of Woody Island to those north of the island. Straits fishos continue to catch a feed, though their focus is shifting to the much larger and slightly more challenging summer whiting down there no doubt.

Snapper from central bay grounds were tough over the neaping tides. Expect better things come the new moon.

Terry Allwood of Flick It Charters fame took time out from Mondy to hit our northern bay reefs with Dane.

Lukas with a brace of fine red emperor from a recent offshore session.

Nice big snapper can be found offshore in numbers. Get out there when the weather lets you, before the springtime current picks up.

Great Sandy Straits Warming into Spring

Pelagic activity within the deeper shipping channels of the Great Sandy Straits is building with the onset of spring. Yellowtail kingfish have been reported hanging around the jetty at Kingfisher Bay Resort, where other pelagics such as mackerel could pay a visit any day. Fishing for flathead and bream can while away the hours between high-speed bites over there, where a wander along the beach with whiting tackle could be productive on bigger tides.

School mackerel have found their way into the mouth of the Mary River. Fishos spinning from the rocks at River Heads have been catching them, albeit only small ones. So many undersized fish some days might warrant retrofitting spoons and slugs with singles in lieu of trebles just to minimise the damage to the baby mackerel. Schoolies are also working the mouth of the Burrum too apparently, so go catch some, or avoid them if you are not a fan.

The creeks of the straits are home to all sorts of estuary predators, including barramundi and threadfin salmon. Blue salmon can be found out the front on the flats and in the channels, in the same waters you will find some of the best grunter at present. Mangrove jacks will be welcoming this warmer weather with attitude, so feel free to pit your skills against some early season red dogs if you are up to the task.

If that seems too daunting, then you can fall back on one of the simplest pleasures of estuarine fishing, and go chase flathead. It is flatty prime time right now as they are mid-spawn mode and quite aggressive. Neap tides can demand a slightly different approach to the springs, but the same techniques will still pin plenty. There is no lure fishery simpler than flathead fishing, so invest in a couple of soft plastics, some matching jig heads and maybe a handful of shallow-diving hard bodies and go target them in the skinny water. You can sight-fish to them in clear waters at this time, so it is extra-enjoyable right now.

Local sand whiting fans will be waiting for the better tides closer to the new moon to hunt their favoured quarry yet again. Pumping yabbies at low tide then soaking them on a flat or near a creek mouth in a rising tide is another of life's simple pleasures. Bag limits are quite easy to achieve, so if you aren't catching then you need to be moving.

Brax Empson dragged this solid black-spotted estuary cod from a local snag on the author's favourite hardbody. Get out of it, Brax!

C'mon Braxxy, we know it's you hiding behind that barra. Let dad catch some on Father's Day for a change can you please.

Jack Mostert has been banging his way around the straits and the lower bay, catching some fine fish like this flatty.

Jack Jones with a big salty on a prawn imitation. A firm favourite of many scopers and others fishos alike.

Rivers Will Be Ultra-Popular This Weekend

This north wind will drive a lot of crews to our local river systems this weekend, where they are bound to do quite well. A good barra bite is expected, to continue on and improve from what has been a particularly good winter bite. Choose the Burrum and you will have ample barra to gawk at on your sounder whilst trying to tempt them. They should be easy enough in all but the areas being flogged relentlessly.

The Burrum's threadies will also be on the chew, and its jacks will fire up a notch with warmer conditions. Having four rivers to choose from can spread the effort on the Burrum system, yet accumulations of fish in some stretches can tend to draw a crowd. Be courteous to those around you and respect the right of those that beat you to a spot. There are oodles of locations you can try in lieu of where others are, and you might even find the motherlode.

Fish the Mary system instead if you prefer. Its bigger fish are a very real drawcard for those that are trophy hunters. Be it barra or threadfin salmon, there is no denying the Mary's bigger fish dwarf most of those elsewhere. Having said that, you will still need to track them down, so trust your sounder and don't waste time on lifeless locations. The threadies and the barra are pretty hyperactive day and night this time of year and will be spurred into action even more-so with this warmer weather.

Clearer waters in both river systems mean you can try multiple different lure options with confidence. Realistic imitations will be appealing to fish enjoying good underwater visibility. Leave the outlandish colours and weird profiles for flood waters later in summer. Try your hand at topwater while the opportunity is so prime. Mimic prawn and/or baitfish with different retrieves to see what they are feeding on. If it is both (which it is) then you can mix it up.

There are many other species you can target in our rivers, and plenty of potential bycatch. Bull sharks are active enough to warrant some effort by those inclined to chase them, whilst also worth avoiding by those trying not to. Prone to snatch larger live baits meant for barra, the baby bulls can be a real handful on barra tackle. Bigger models are more likely to home in on hooked fish, as are some serious groper in certain waters.

You can have some fun just chasing flathead in clear waters within the mid-lower reaches of the Burrum or the Mary. Whiting are an option in the lower Susan in a week, and you can expect another good run of large sand whiting in the Burrum and the Gregory come the new moon. Bream will be there if they excite you, as will greenback tailor most likely, and improving numbers of grunter.

So, there is much to look forward to this weekend, regardless of the so-called 'dreaded northerly'. That breeze only annoys open water and bay fishos. Estuary fishos welcome it with open arms. Happy Father's Day to all the fishing dads out there. May your Sunday be extra-special and full of fishy family memories to cherish forever.

Good luck out there y'all …… Jase

Jacko put this fine jewie on the deck with the aid of Lowrance Active Target tech. This is a very good month to catch jewies locally.

The Brown kids with the spoils of a recent crabbing mission. This may be the 'worst' time to catch muddies, but they just keep coming this year.

entry.title: Fisho's Weekly Fishing Report – 28th August, 2026
entry.content:
Shaun from Saltwater Playground with a solid Westin Swim-munching red bass from the shoals east of Breaksea Spit.

Say Goodbye to the Winter that Barely Was

After a 4-week hiatus due to considerable ongoing pain, it is good to be back in the chair bringing you the latest from the fishing scene here on the Fraser Coast. Lots has happened over the past 4 weeks; from our biggest and most successful annual clearance sale at the shop, to seasonal changes and migratory movements of our piscatorial friends.

The AFTA annual trade show at the Gold Coast last week showcased an incredible array of future fishing must-haves that we are frantically ordering at present. We will select only the best and most applicable for our region from the multitude of new offerings, ensuring you don't miss out and get the edge on the fish.

Our loss is your gain at this time too, as we have to move-on perfectly good product to make way for all the flash new gear. Dump bins will be bristling with discounted product in coming weeks, whilst select items will be stashed for the upcoming major sales period - Black Friday into Xmas. Keep your eyes peeled for instore bargains as you wander the store sussing out all the new post-AFTA goodies. There will be much to get excited about!

Before reviewing your fishing options; a quick look at the weather as usual. Hasn't this been a mild winter! Warmer nights than expected have been very welcome, even though often triggered by unseasonal cloud cover and occasionally annoying precipitation at times. Last winter was notable due to the significant prevalence of dry westerly winds, yet this year, the westerlies' absence has been conspicuous. More onshore winds than anticipated continue to prevail as we see out a most enjoyable winter in God's country.

Today's 10-15 knot south-easter is set to prevail into Saturday. Probably more 15 knots than 10, but vastly better than Sunday's offering of 15-20 knots from the same direction. A shower is possible Sunday, and maybe again early in the working week, when the breeze is expected to ease gradually day by day. Tending northerly and quite light by mid-week, it is bound to feel very much like spring has arrived.

Tonight's full moon sees the peak of yet another lunar cycle. As the moon wanes thereafter and the tides diminish, a number of local fisheries will lose their appeal. Make the most of this weekend folks, it should be a good one on many fronts, regardless of the less-than-ideal weather.

Liam Aldridge caught this 97cm golden trevally at the Pt Vernon artificial reef on a rather chilly morning earlier this month.

Large cobia remain fairly constant bycatch in the northern and central bay.

Urangan Pier Fishery Improves into Spring

Considering the past 4 weeks on the Urangan Pier, unless you are a dedicated bream fan or you timed your assaults right for the passing longtail tuna, then you didn't miss out on much. Baitfish have been there, but 'port hole' herring have outnumbered 'greenbacks' quite consistently. That remains the case, yet pelagic activity has certainly improved over the past week or so.

School mackerel have been somewhat consistent, albeit very small. Undersized fish have been more common than legal models, with the best fish barely 55cm models. This is highly typical of this time of year. Fleeting visits from small numbers of equally-disappointing chopper tailor were barely notable during August, with none keen to settle in for any period.

The return of a small pod of yellowtail kingfish has created some excitement amongst pier regulars. Fish in the 10-15 kilo class have been reported by some, whilst others claim the fish are even bigger than that. Incidentally, Kingfisher Bay Resort's jetty has also enjoyed a visit from kingies recently, so a handful of land-based fishos have had the opportunity to test their tackle on these southern bruisers.

Gin-clear water has created fantastic sight-fishing opportunities for those seeking flathead beneath Urangan Pier. Pike can be caught with enough effort, and continue to prove themselves as the number one livie for pier flatties. Bream fishos are still securing a modest feed from the planks, but their days are numbered. A peak in activity this full moon will probably satiate them as they replace bream terminals with gear more suited to the whiting fishery about to burst onto the scene.

John Brown avoided the sharks long enough to catch a trout nearly as big as the one on his shirt.

Bar-cheek coral trout will be on the bite in the northern bay if you can get there and find a spot without attending sharks.

Beaches Come Alive with Whiting as Spring Arrives

The onset of spring means whiting time for our town beaches and the Urangan Pier. Often kicking off late August, the run of 'summer' whiting from Urangan to Torquay is a popular event for the family fisho. The kids can have a ball catching quality whiting from the beach end of the pier, from the groynes at Shelly Beach and along local north-facing beachfronts.

Bigger tides are the go, so if you miss out this weekend, then prepare yourself for the approach of the next new moon. No-one has been in bragging about beach whiting as yet, so it looks like a belated start (like so many other fisheries these days it seems). In the meantime, consider some effort during any spells of northerly wind that create the necessary turbulence and cover that cruising schools of whiting need to forage closer to shore in such clear waters. Until consistent northerlies 'dirty' our waters a tad, efforts after dark will be most successful.

To date, the beachscape most consistently giving up a feed or some fun has been the stretches out at Toogoom. Currently weed-free, yet benefitting from the recover of sea grasses, there has been whiting and bream schooling out there at times. The creeks out that way have been visited by the same fish, joining flathead, queenfish, small golden and giant trevally and even a couple of cool wintertime barramundi.

Persistent onshore winds have not been conducive to better fishing down along the Booral Flats. Those vast muddy stretches can produce ample whiting and flathead along with blue salmon, grunter and occasional threadies, but offshore winds are favourable for any consistency. This past month has not offered the best conditions down there.

Beach whiting will improve in size in coming weeks. Boaties are averaging 30-35cm locally, and even bigger in the Gregory.

Kade Whittle went to book week at his school dressed as Jacko from Fishos. Very funny young man!

Latest News from Our Inshore Reef Fishery

As the ever-consistent grassy sweetlip population that feeds so many families wanes into late winter, hungry fishos have been plying for snapper, coral trout and estuary cod with mixed results. It would be nice to finally say that the sharks have backed off (like they sometimes do August-September) but alas, no such luck so far.

Bay snapper reports post-closure have been less than impressive, yet there have been some very nice knobbies caught all the same. Weather issues, prevalent whales and shark depredation have all been factors playing on the minds of local fishos that would've otherwise been chafing at the bit to get amongst the knobbies since the 16th August season opening.

There is plenty of appeal, tides and moon wise, for inshore forays this weekend if you can handle a bit of weather. Put in some effort hopping plastics over snapper haunts lousy with baitfish and hopefully the bites will come. Avoid persisting should the noahs be present, as you have many locations where you can confidently expect snapper to be lingering this time of year.

Whilst you might find knobbies on the grounds off the Burrum coast, across the banks or around reefs in our shipping channels; it is the numerous reefs and weedy outcrops in Platypus Bay and the central bay that are likely to be most consistent at this time. Be aware, that snot weed has been reported at places in Platypus Bay, so move elsewhere if it affects you (it is not everywhere).

Stuart had his hands full with this big cod. All cod even close to this size are best released to keep our reefs in good nick.

Brad Anderson with a fair chunk of estuary cod. It is more important than ever to release these brutes if they aren't suffering barotrauma.

Whales are ridiculously prolific in Platypus Bay, and much of the wider bay. This fact is playing havoc with more and more boaties accustomed to night-time travel in the bay. Be wary and keep a good watch during daylight and limit your travel in the evenings. Kick back and enjoy the spectacle that the whales offer and involve the family when you can. We are truly blessed to have such a phenomenal experience on offer in our backyard.

Keep an eye out for the New Zealand fur seal that remains at large somewhere along the vast Platypus Bay stretch of beach. Last seen recently at Awinya Creek (that we know of), it is great to hear that it has survived the attention of the tiger sharks spotted cruising nearby when it first arrived and was showing signs of a past wounding. Word of another similar seal on the eastern surf-side beach of Fraser makes one wish for a reunion between the two, so they can cruise back south together perhaps.

The demise of another humpback a couple of weeks ago wide of Arch Cliffs created a spectacle for those that spotted it. Attended by multiple large tiger sharks at the time, it was still floating prior to apparently sinking somewhere north-west of the 6 Mile. Pictures doing the rounds of an incredibly fat great white shark spotted 11 miles off Arch Cliffs thereafter has folks debating whether its extraordinary girth is the result of pregnancy or gorging on blubber. Most likely the latter if these critters documented tendency to overeat is considered.

As if Hervey Bay sharks aren't already fat enough! Deceased humpbacks have fattened them further this winter.

Ben's jewfish came up short. A cut this straight suggests the taxman was one of our bigger models.

Trevally Dominate the Bay Pelagic Scene

Whilst scattered schools of tuna can be found in Hervey Bay waters, it is the small schools of very large fish known to haunt the straits this time of year that get a few folks excited. Without specific reports from the area to confirm, it is still worth noting their tendency to turn up off Inskip Point south of Fraser at this time (in case you are heading down that way). Not lots of tuna, but very large models full of steam and a never-die attitude when hooked.

Much easier to find (and equally as hard to avoid if you aren't a fan) are the vast hordes of trevally that inundate our baitfish-rich reef systems this time of year. There will be ample goldies and a few of their cousins inshore around shipwrecks, other artificial reefs and local ledges, but it is the waters of Platypus Bay and the northern bay that truly come alive with the greatest biomass of assorted trevors.

Clans such as the goldies, diamonds, brassies, giants, bludgers and quite a few others cloud sounder screens in arches at places such as the Gutters and (to a lesser extent) off Rooneys. Large enough to give you a workout and ever-willing to pounce on jigs, softies, live baits and well-presented dead offerings, these trevors can be exhausting fun for family fishos and those not hell-bent on catching reefies.

Hordes of their smaller brethren, plus schools of sizeable goldies, diamonds and brassies, dominate many a reefy patch in Platypus Bay at the same time. Fantastic fun for the smaller kids cutting their teeth on spinning and jigging tackle. Such fun often interspersed with moments of sheer exhilaration and awe as oversized cobia rock up to see what all the commotion is about. The big cobes are a still a northern bay staple (for now) and will feature randomly in catches late into spring.

The GTs that lurk on the shallower prominent bommies offshore east of Breaksea Spit have been on the rampage lately. Heavy casting tackle is paramount to deny these brutes sanctuary from the gnarly reefs below when hooked whilst dancing big stickies or blooping poppers across the surface above.

A couple more recent juvenile dogtooth tuna captures from the shoal country out there reflects their presence more consistently as they are discovered by chance. Who knows, maybe the odd monumental bust-up on the shoals is a doggy a bit bigger than these pups. The spaniards have been hard to find out lately apparently, yet reports from Waddy Point only a month ago suggest they were down that way harassing tailor.

The mackerel scene close inshore is a bit hit and miss at present. Pulses of small (often undersized) schoolies are migrating into the bay and beyond into the straits. Small schoolies are being spun from the rocks at River Heads for example, where the abundant herring have been a drawcard for them and tailor. Time will see a better class of fish arrive, with spaniards hot on their heels. In the meantime, look for broadies down the straits if you are keen.

Saltwater Playground clients have been catching bruiser giant trevally off the bommies east of Breaksea.

Head for the shoal country off Breaksea when the current is racing and you can catch GTs like Saltwater Playground clients.

Rivers Clearing and Many Fish on the Move

The River Heads area can be productive for more than just the usual estuarine species at this time of year. Cleaner waters appeal to the expected run of bream, flathead, jewfish and blue salmon for both land-based and boat-based fishos, yet pelagics and even stray reef fish can be caught in the vicinity too. Fishing the river mouth with the right baits or lures could see you connect to squire and blackall after dark, often encountered by those otherwise hoping for jewfish or cod.

Up-river migratory movements of apex estuarine predators have already commenced, but is early days yet for the largest biomasses of fish. Reduced gill-netting opportunity will see their passage unimpeded until they cross the boundary upstream that still permits this activity. Whilst the pros are in position and working hard to earn their keep, there are fish you can intercept before they get them.

Grunter are on the move, yet also schooling in apparent spawning aggregations on the flats just beyond the river's immediate influence. Fun times for flats fishos abound should they trip over swirling masses of grunter, often nearby to dizzying swirls of blue salmon. Light tackle often needing a spell should the largest of the blues be encountered, as anyone who has experienced this phenomenon can attest.

Threadies of immense proportions can be found within the Mary River, as well as down the straits. A lesser (but ever-growing and improving) class of fish in the Burrum system offering just as much fun when found in numbers. Its all about big fish and less of them in select stretches of the Mary at present, but those fish will be joined by many more in coming weeks and months. Smaller threadies are abundant in smaller systems and easier to catch than ever.

Dane hitched a ride upriver with Logan and caught this ripper thready on the new BKK Hyperlatch jighead.

Threadfin salmon numbers will increase and they will get easier and easier to catch in coming weeks.

The 2026 winter barra season was a beauty. Some targeted trophy fish with livescope and bettered PBs one after the other. Folks more accustomed to snag-bashing old school caught numbers too, in a winter season warmer than most on record. Interest in our barra fishery will increase dramatically with warming waters, so crowds and traffic will have its effects. Luckily, our major river systems are healthy and productive, and the straits (including Fraser's western creeks) offer ample action.

The Burrum is effectively gillnet-free these days and will see masses of recreational fishos this spring. All four rivers offer options galore for the likes of barra, threadies and jacks, whilst jewfish are a chance, and blues and big tarpon are a distraction. We should see the long-awaited return of schools of queenfish and river GTs (if they haven't done so already). Grunter will continue an upstream march and settle briefly in favourable stretches.

Tailor are a possible target for those favouring the lower reaches. Bigger tides over the coming month could see very solid fish caught, particularly at night. Bream can be found in numbers well downstream, yet quite a few chunky models are also taking baits and lures well upstream already too. Flathead are abundant and stonker whiting are being reported in the Gregory. Bag limits may be rare in there, but who needs 30 whiting if they are bettering the 40cm mark.

Local whiting fishos back down this way have been bagging out on summeries regularly for about 6 weeks now, whenever the weather enables access to the flats and creeks they favour. Evening sessions have still been the best by far, as clear waters inhibit the daytime feeding actions of larger whiting in some areas. That will change with the onset of spring and northerly winds, but at that same time can come the issue with dislodged snot weed and its inherent challenges in a few popular areas.

Coxy with a sample of the grunter you can catch as they migrate back upriver. Find them on the flats and they are even more fun.

Chewy that works for us at Fishos makes flies for impoundment barra and loves testing them at Mondy.

Latest Reports from Fraser's Surf Scene

A month ago, I reported on a lack lustre fishing scene on Fraser's surf side, just as a big southerly blow trashed the beaches over there and put paid to the fishing briefly. Tailor were hard to find pre-blow, but a week thereafter, there were reports of decent schools of choppers making their way up the island. Hearing word of occasional short-lived success in weeks since, but being unable to report on it, I can finally bring you the latest goss from locals on the island.

Beach travel at low tide right now is generally excellent. There are wash-outs at a few creek crossings however, and they are pretty nasty ones, so watch out. You may not see the drop-offs until you are right on top of them, so monitor your island map and identify the creeks (miniscule as they might be) so you can slow down as you approach. The locals know where they are. First-timers and occasional visitors find them as they drive, so be careful.

High tide travel is more challenging and slower, but possible. The beach is pretty lumpy above the mid-tide mark, meaning high tide gutter formations that tailor fishos could be potentially returning to when the time is right. The island's sand access tracks are quite reasonable, even though there has been, and still is, quite big numbers of people on the island. Just enough showery weather to harden the sand has helped, and the graders etc have been to work on the Kingfisher to Eurong track that was particularly nasty prior.

Pippies have been pretty easy to find along various stretches of beach. The massive abundance down south beyond Dilli 2 months ago has moved on. Look for 'push-ups' as you travel and you will secure your bag limit of pippies enroute to your next gutter potentially. Wormers are working the island and doing well. Recreational wormers can pull a handy supply without too much hassle, and the worms are fat and clean.

Jewfish have been the big buzz amongst crews in the central sector of the island, even though it is only a few fishos catching them. Fish in the 80-90cm size range have been caught often enough to warrant a little extra effort from those getting word of their presence. Success over this full moon might only be curtailed by the onshore south-easter that is building to 20 knots.

Worth mentioning yet again, is the fact that there are no 'silver jewfish' to be caught from the beaches of Fraser Island. Any jewfish caught over there will be a mulloway and must be at least 75cm in length to be legally kept. Fisheries must get sick of arguing this fact with folks insisting the 45cm silver jew minimum size applies to beach-caught jew. It doesn't!

Catches of tailor are yet to be consistent, but there have been encouraging moments. Some crews have headed over and failed miserably, only to hear of the success of others after their return. Such are the vagaries of surf fishing. The best reports to date have been from the Maheno north. Undersized choppers are mixed with barely legal models in some schools, so be selective and mobile if alternative gutters are within your scope.

A few larger tailor caught up Ngkala way one week were encouraging, but then they disappeared.
